title: OPERATION OPEN LINE
skeleton: a garrison must keep one briefly-revived interstellar relay transmitting through a deliberate assault whose entire purpose is to silence the call for help before it lands, where the station is both the only objective and a wasting asset whose transmit window closes on its own decay clock, so the crux is holding the relay sending rather than holding any ground
inspiration: the besieged signal station racing to get one message out before the wire is cut — Rorke's Drift heliograph and the last cable from a falling outpost, 19th century
situation:
Nobody on {WORLD} expected the relay to wake. The HPG on the {DISTRICT} massif went dark with all the others in 3132. For {OFFLINE_YEARS} years the militia guarded a dead station out of habit. Then a ComStar repair crew got it partly working again: three adepts and a salvaged tuning core. It will not last. The techs are blunt. The patched capacitor stack has about {RELAY_DAYS} days of transmit life left, and every message sent shortens that. For those few days, {WORLD} is the only world in the district that can call for help.

That is exactly why raiders are coming. Your employer is {EMPLOYER}, the planetary council, and your contact is {NPC:employer-contact}. The council sees the danger clearly. A world that can call for help is a world that gets help. A raider who lets that call go out has to face whatever answers it. {NPC:intel-source} already has the enemy's flight path. One reinforced raider battalion will land within {GROUND_HOURS} hours, running dark, and their heavy machines are aimed at the massif road, not the capital or the farms. They are not here to loot {WORLD}. They are here to silence the relay before it costs them.

The terrain problem is the massif itself. The relay sits at the top of a single switchback road that climbs 1,400 meters of terraced slope. That same chokepoint made it easy to defend in the League era, and it traps the defender now. There is one road up, wide enough for assault machines but only one machine wide at three hairpin turns. The relay's fusion plant and dish array sit exposed on the summit shelf. Below, attacking armor is forced into narrow ground the garrison has had a century to range. Hold the three hairpins and you hold the mountain. Hold the summit and keep the dish turning, and you hold the district's only voice.

Your garrison: 2 militia rifle battalions, an armor company of 11 mixed vehicles, and whatever your own unit brought. The message the council wants sent is already written and waiting to transmit. It is worthless the moment the dish stops turning, and the enemy knows this hardware better than the council does.

objectives.primary: Keep the relay transmitting until its power runs out. Send the council's relief request, and every follow-up message, and get them acknowledged before the station fails or falls.
objectives.secondary: Keep the massif road and summit shelf undamaged. A cratered road or a wrecked dish denies {WORLD} the relay just as surely as the raiders would.
objectives.bonus: Identify who is paying the raiders, using their signals and salvage. Gather evidence the relief force can act on when it arrives.

complications.name: The Dying Stack
complications.text: The patched capacitor bank holds about {RELAY_DAYS} days of transmit life if used carefully, and every message spends some of it. Combat shock, near-misses, and an emergency reactor shutdown all cost extra. Only the three adepts know how much is truly left.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Every transmission draws from a tracked relay-life pool. Heavy fighting near the summit drains it faster. When the pool hits zero, the relay is dead no matter who holds the ground. An emergency reactor shutdown costs a fixed chunk of the pool plus a restart delay.

complications.name: The One Road
complications.text: The massif has one switchback road with three hairpin turns, each only one machine wide. It is the garrison's strength and its trap. Supplies and wounded travel it too, and a blocked hairpin cuts the summit off from the valley below.
complications.mechanicalEffect: All ground movement to and from the summit uses this road. A wreck or demolition at any hairpin closes it for a repair interval. While it is closed, the summit garrison fights on what it has and cannot be reinforced or relieved from below.

complications.name: They Know the Dish
complications.text: The raiders studied the station before they came. Their fire plan singles out the dish array and the reactor, not the bunkers around them. They want to kill the relay, not the garrison. Once the relay is silenced, they leave.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Enemy direct fire targets the dish array and fusion reactor before it targets troops or armor. Damage to either slows or stops transmission no matter how the rest of the fight is going. Defending the hardware pulls strength away from defending the line.

decisionPoints.name: The Shape of the Defense
decisionPoints.context: The relay must keep sending for days against a force built to silence it fast. The garrison is too small to be strong everywhere, and the dish is more fragile than any patch of ground. How you set up now decides what the assault runs into.

options.title: Hold the Summit, Forward
advantages: Keeps enemy heavy weapons off the dish for as long as the road holds
The relay transmits freely while the fight stays down on the terraces
Puts your best machines where the terrain favors the defender
disadvantages: This spends strength on ground, and one lost hairpin traps the whole forward force below the dish it is protecting
Every hour of close fighting on the approach drains the relay pool through combat shock and reactor-shutdown risk
If the line breaks, it breaks with the garrison on the wrong side of the summit
options.consequence: The relay stays clear as long as the road holds, and the whole fight becomes the road. You are betting the relay's remaining life on holding the hairpins. The raiders are betting they can crack one before the message lands.

costs.resource: your reserve, committed forward to the hairpins, leaving no force to retake the summit if the line is turned
costs.risk: the forward line fails below the dish, trapping its defenders under the objective they were sent to hold

options.title: Hold the Summit, Tight
advantages: A tight ring around the dish and reactor means the hardware is never left undefended, even at the worst moment
Shortens the line to what the garrison can actually hold, and shortens the supply road behind it
Keeps a real reserve in hand for the summit itself
disadvantages: Gives up the terraces and lower hairpins, so the enemy reaches firing range of the dish whenever they choose
The relay transmits under fire, with every message a gamble against enemy guns
A tight perimeter under steady bombardment burns the relay's remaining life fast, through combat shock and reactor-shutdown risk
options.consequence: You trade the approach for a solid shield over the hardware, and the fight becomes a siege of the summit shelf. The dish keeps turning inside the wire, for exactly as long as both the wire and the capacitor stack last.

costs.resource: the terraces and lower road, given up by choice, to be retaken later or not at all
costs.risk: enemy fire reaches the dish early, and the relay pool burns under bombardment the perimeter cannot stop

options.title: Send Now, Hold After
advantages: Use the relay hard in the first window: every queued message, every district, sent several times over, before the assault reaches firing range
If the calls land before the dish dies, you can lose the station and still win the mission
Removes the raiders' whole reason to spare the hardware
disadvantages: Spending it all up front empties most of the relay pool in days, leaving nothing for the follow-ups, corrections, or second requests the relief will need
You then hold a dead station through the rest of the assault for nothing but the ground
Once the raiders know the message is out, they fight to wipe you out, not to silence you
options.consequence: You get the word out while you still can, and accept that the rest of the battle is fought over a dead station. The relief is called on the first day. Whether it arrives in time to find anyone alive is a separate clock.

costs.resource: the relay-life pool, spent down to almost nothing in the opening window, with no transmit capacity left for the days after
costs.risk: the message lands and the station dies, and the garrison defends ground with nothing left to bargain with but its own survival

decisionPoints.name: The Reactor Decision
decisionPoints.context: Mid-assault, raider sappers reach the fusion reactor that powers the dish. You can shut it down and lock it: safe, but the relay goes dark for the restart. Or you can keep it running under threat, transmitting until the moment it is captured or breached.

options.title: Shut Down and Lock
advantages: The reactor survives, the dish survives, and the relay can come back if the summit holds
Denies the raiders a working transmitter to capture and use for themselves
Buys time to clear the sappers without a live reactor on the firing line
disadvantages: The relay goes dark for the full restart, meaning hours of silence in a window measured in days
A mid-assault shutdown is a gap the raiders may read as the station already dead, and push harder
The restart spends relay-life the garrison may not get back
options.consequence: You go silent to save the equipment. If the summit holds through the restart, the relay speaks again once it comes back. If it does not, the last thing the district heard was a message cut off halfway.

costs.resource: hours of dead air during the restart, plus a fixed chunk of relay-life, spent to keep the option of speaking later
costs.risk: the silence reads as death, and the raiders commit to the summit believing the job is already done

options.title: Keep It Running
advantages: The relay keeps transmitting through the sapper fight, with no gap, no restart, and every second of the window used
Forces the raiders to capture the reactor intact or breach it themselves, both slow and both costly
The message keeps landing while the fight for the hardware is still undecided
disadvantages: A breached or damaged reactor on the summit shelf is a disaster for everyone on it, garrison included
Fighting around a live reactor limits the garrison's own heavy fire as much as the enemy's
If the raiders capture the reactor intact, they hold the transmitter and the advantage both
options.consequence: You keep the relay alive by fighting next to a live reactor under attack. The window stays open, and so does the worst case: one breach and the summit is gone for good.

costs.resource: the garrison's freedom to fire on the summit shelf, limited by the live reactor it is protecting
costs.risk: a reactor breach in the close fight destroys the relay, the garrison, and the mountain all at once

options.title: Rig It to Blow
advantages: Wire the dish array and tuning core with charges, so if the summit falls the raiders get wreckage, not a working transmitter
Removes the enemy's reason to capture the hardware intact, turning the assault from surgical to brute-force
A real self-destruct is a bargaining chip: the relay speaks for {WORLD} or it speaks for no one
disadvantages: If the rigged dish goes off by accident, shellfire, or a panicked hand, the garrison ends its own mission
Putting charges on the district's only voice is a call the council did not authorize and may not forgive
Once it is wired, every near-miss is a coin flip on the objective
options.consequence: You make the relay a hostage you hold against yourself. The raiders can no longer win by capturing the dish, only by forcing you to blow it or by holding the wrecked shelf. The line between defending it and destroying it gets very thin.

costs.resource: the relay itself, turned into a demolition charge the garrison must now guard against accidents
costs.risk: a wired objective under bombardment is one stray round away from a self-inflicted mission failure

entries.event: Ground lookouts spot unscheduled drive flares coming down a steep descent. The profile reads as one reinforced raider battalion. The alarm goes to the summit by landline, so the relay is not wasted on warning itself.
Militia move to their assembly points and the armor company moves to the mouth of the terraces. The three adepts open the first transmit window with the council's relief request.
The raider heavy element lands on the valley floor and starts the road march to the massif. Light elements peel off toward the lower terraces to pin the garrison's screen.
First contact at the lowest hairpin. The enemy's fire plan shows immediate interest in the summit hardware: ranging shots fall on the dish shelf, not the bunkers.
The raider main body commits to the switchback. This is the earliest point at which a lost hairpin can cut off the summit.
Expected turning point: if the road has not held, the raiders reach firing range of the dish. From here on, the relay transmits under their guns.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The relay has about {RELAY_DAYS} days of transmit life, and the assault is built to end sooner. The hard limit is the moment the capacitor stack fails or the dish stops turning, whichever comes first. After that, {WORLD} is silent again, whatever relief was called is the relief it gets, and the garrison is fighting for a mountain instead of a message. Every message sent gets a world a hearing. Every message not sent in time was the one that mattered.

opforSketch.composition: A reinforced raider consortium battalion, salvage-heavy: a BattleMech company of mixed light-to-heavy machines (Regular, with a Veteran command lance) leading, 1-2 combat-vehicle companies including sappers and a demolition section (this is the combined-arms weight — armor and engineers canalizing up the terraces), and motorized raider infantry for the close work on the summit. 1-2 Union- or Overlord-class DropShips. They field a deliberate counter-signals element tasked at the dish. Behavioral breakpoint: the heavy element breaks contact and re-forms if the relief call is confirmed landed AND the dish still stands — at that point silencing failed and the arithmetic has soured.
opforSketch.behavior: Surgical, not greedy. The consortium fights to silence the relay on a clock, not to take {WORLD}: it presses the road hard while the station can still call, accepts costs it would never pay for loot, and disengages the moment the message is out or the hardware is denied. Sappers go for the plant and dish; the command lance goes for the hairpins. They came to make a world quiet, and they leave when it is quiet or when staying stops being worth it.

forks.name: OPERATION ANSWERED CALL
forks.trigger: The relief request and its confirmations are sent and acknowledged before the relay fails, the summit and dish held intact.
forks.consequence: Something answers. A relieving force jumps in-system on the strength of the call the garrison kept alive — and the unit, knowing the ground and the enemy better than the newcomers, is asked to guide the link-up and the counterstroke that throws the consortium off {WORLD} for good.

forks.name: OPERATION DEAD AIR
forks.trigger: The relay is silenced — stack failed, dish destroyed, or summit lost — before the call is acknowledged.
forks.consequence: {WORLD} is mute again and on its own. The consortium, having done what it came for, settles into the unhurried looting of a world that cannot call anyone, and the garrison fights the rest of a siege no one off-planet will ever hear about.

forks.name: OPERATION CROSSED WIRE
forks.trigger: The raiders capture the dish or tuning core intact, or the relay's true failure date leaks to them mid-assault.
forks.consequence: The transmitter changes hands with life left in it. The consortium can now send as easily as silence — a false all-clear over {WORLD}'s own relay, waving off the relief or summoning a friend of theirs — and the garrison must retake or destroy the voice it was hired to protect, against an enemy holding the high summit.

storyElementSeed: Inside the relay hut, between bursts, an adept tapes a strip of cardboard over the capacitor readout so the gun crews carrying ammunition past the door will stop asking how many windows are left. The number on the strip is yesterday's. She does not change it.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no munitions depot under contract. A front-loaded defense burns reserve ammunition the garrison cannot replace. Either add 12,000 C-bills of open-market stock bought before the assault, or fight the second half of the siege on what the militia magazines hold.

You have no engineers of your own. Militia sappers rig the charges under a tech's supervision. Add 1 day to wire it safely, and accept a higher chance of accidental detonation on every near-miss until it is armed.

title: OPERATION COLD LAMP
skeleton: a relief column must reach a string of isolated outposts strung along a single seasonal ice route before the thaw makes the road impassable for the rest of the year, choosing which posts on the failing road to relieve when it cannot reach them all, where the road itself is the wasting asset and the enemy times its blocks to the melt rather than to the column
inspiration: the winter ice-road relief runs to cut-off northern settlements, and the Ladoga ice road to a besieged city, mid-20th century
situation:
{WORLD}'s northern reach lives and dies by the freeze. For four months of the long winter, the {DISTRICT} ice road runs 600 kilometers across the frozen sounds and tundra, linking the rim-mining outposts to the smelter towns and the spaceport in the south. For the other eight months the route is open water, bottomless muskeg, and nothing. The Blackout cut the orbital lifts that once made the road optional. Now it is the only way in. Your employer is {EMPLOYER}, the {DISTRICT} mining consortium, and your contact is {NPC:employer-contact}. They kept five outposts staffed through the winter on the promise of a supply run before the thaw. The run is now overdue, the thaw has come early, and the road has only days left, not the weeks the schedule assumed.

The consortium's distress messages, carried south by sled, are grim and specific. Note that these reports are 6 to 14 days old, so treat them as a starting point, not the current state. Five outposts, {OUTPOST_TOTAL} people, fuel and food figured to the original relief date and no further. The ice road is already failing from the south. The first 80 kilometers are slush and cracking ice, good for wheeled and tracked vehicles for about {ROAD_DAYS} more days before the sounds open. After that the outposts are cut off until the next freeze, which several of them will not last to see. Your column, made up of the consortium's heavy haulers, fuel trucks, and your own machines for muscle, cannot reach all five before the road dies. The route is the clock, and the clock is melting.

The enemy is the second clock. A raider band the consortium calls the Hoarfrost has wintered on the reach for two seasons, living off what it takes from the outposts it does not quite destroy. They know the ice road better than the consortium does, and they have read the same early thaw you have. {NPC:intel-source} reports the band is set to block the road's chokepoints, timed not to when the column arrives but to when the melt makes a block hardest to clear and a detour impossible. A blown ice bridge in deep winter is an inconvenience. The same bridge dropped three days before the thaw strands everyone north of it for a year. The Hoarfrost are not trying to beat the column. They are trying to let the road beat it.

The terrain problem is the Narrows: a 9-kilometer crossing of a tidal sound where the ice road runs on sea ice over moving water. It is the one point on the route with no land route around it, and the first stretch to fail. Past the Narrows lie the three northern outposts; before it, the two that are only desperate. Cross the Narrows late and the column is stuck north of a melting bridge with its way home dissolving behind it. Never cross it and three outposts are simply written off by the math.

objectives.primary: Reach as many of the five outposts as the failing road allows. Deliver fuel, food, and medical supplies, and pull out the most exposed people, before the thaw closes the route.
objectives.secondary: Bring the column home intact. Leave no haulers stranded north of a failed crossing, and do not add the relief force to the list of the cut-off.
objectives.bonus: Break the Hoarfrost's grip on the reach by taking the band's fuel cache or its leaders, so next winter's run is only a race and not a siege as well.

complications.name: The Melting Road
complications.text: The ice road fails from the south and from the edges inward, faster than the schedule and faster with every warm hour. The {ROAD_DAYS}-day estimate is a hope. The real number is whatever the sounds decide, and they decide day by day.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A road-life clock counts down each day of the operation. Warm weather speeds it up; cold snaps slow it down. Crossing any chokepoint late costs extra clock. When a road segment's clock runs out, that segment is impassable for the rest of the mission, and anything north of it is stuck.

complications.name: Posts on the Same Road
complications.text: Five outposts, one road, and fuel and food running out on different dates. The column cannot reach all five in time. Choosing which to help is choosing who waits and who never gets reached at all.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each outpost has its own supply clock and its own distance down the road. Time spent relieving one is time not spent reaching another. An outpost not reached by the date its supplies run out suffers worsening losses, which the consortium counts against the contract.

complications.name: Blocks Timed to the Thaw
complications.text: The Hoarfrost do not block the column, they block the road, and they pick the hour that makes the block hardest to undo. A bridge dropped near the thaw cannot be bypassed, repaired, or recrossed.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Raider demolition and ambush events hit chokepoints, timed to the road-life clock rather than to where the column is. A block sprung late in a segment's life may close it for good. Clearing or bridging one costs road-clock the column cannot get back.

decisionPoints.name: The Narrows Crossing
decisionPoints.context: The three northern outposts are the most desperate, and they lie past the Narrows, the first crossing to fail. Crossing it reaches the worst-off but bets the column's return on sea ice that is already softening. Refusing it writes off three posts to keep the road home.

options.title: Cross Heavy and Fast
advantages: Reaches all three northern outposts, the people with the least fuel and the least time
A fast, heavy push beats the Hoarfrost's block if it gets across before the band can drop the Narrows
The boldest delivery the consortium could ask for, and the one that saves the most lives if it works
disadvantages: The whole column ends up north of a melting crossing, its return riding on the ice lasting a few days longer than it should
If the Narrows fails or is dropped behind the column, the relief force joins the very people it came to save
Heavy haulers on softening sea ice can break through and sink, with no enemy involved
options.consequence: You gamble your own way home on the Narrows holding twice, once going and once coming back. Either the three northern posts live, or the relief force dies with them, and the ice decides which.

costs.resource: the return crossing, staked on sea ice the column has already driven over once and warmed by driving it
costs.risk: a failed or dropped Narrows strands the entire column in the north until next freeze, turning a rescue into a second siege

options.title: Stage at the Narrows
advantages: Cross light, with fuel sledges and a security element only, and keep the heavy column and its way home on the safe side
The northern posts get enough to survive, even if not enough to evacuate, and the column is never fully committed
Keeps the option to pull back south the moment the road turns
disadvantages: A light crossing can resupply but cannot evacuate, so the northern posts are kept alive in place, waiting for a rescue that may never get a second chance
Splitting the force cuts your strength in half on both sides of a sound the Hoarfrost are watching
The light element across the Narrows is the most cut-off unit on the reach
options.consequence: You buy the northern posts time without betting the whole force on the ice. It is the careful answer and the incomplete one. Nobody north of the Narrows is saved, only kept alive, and keeping them alive has its own deadline.

costs.resource: the column's strength, split by sending a light element across a failing crossing while the main body waits south
costs.risk: a thaw or a block cuts off the light element, with no heavy force on its side of the sound able to reach it

options.title: Write Off the North
advantages: Put everything into the two southern outposts, which are reachable, can be evacuated, and sit on solid road for a few more days
The column stays whole, stays on the safe side, and comes home for certain
The Hoarfrost's Narrows block no longer matters, because the column was never going to cross it
disadvantages: Three outposts and the people in them are abandoned on purpose, not lost by bad luck, and both the consortium and the survivors will remember it
Gives up the northern reach to the Hoarfrost for the season and likely for good
The bonus of breaking the band is far harder with half the reach given up
options.consequence: You save what you can be sure of and turn your back on what you might have saved. Two posts come home. The other three become a line in the report and a grievance the consortium carries into next winter's contract.

costs.resource: the three northern outposts and everyone in them, given up to the math
costs.risk: a decision that is both correct and unforgivable, made in public where the survivors can count the cost

decisionPoints.name: The Hoarfrost Block
decisionPoints.context: The band springs its block at a chokepoint with the road-clock already low: a blown span or a dug-in ambush across the only route. Clearing it costs precious road-life. Going around, where there is a way around, costs more. And the band sits between the column and an outpost that cannot wait.

options.title: Force the Block
advantages: Smash through fast and keep the column moving on the dying road, because speed is all you have left
A hard fight now is cheaper than a detour the road-clock cannot afford
Breaking the block at the chokepoint may break the Hoarfrost's grip on that whole stretch
disadvantages: A pitched fight at a chokepoint burns road-clock during the fighting as well as the clearing
The band chose this ground, so forcing it means attacking a prepared position with the melt at your back
Casualties and damaged haulers slow every kilometer after
options.consequence: You pay in blood and hours to keep the road open under you. The block breaks or it does not, and either way the thaw kept running while the guns fired.

costs.resource: road-life clock spent in the fight, plus haulers and machines damaged forcing a prepared position
costs.risk: a slow fight at the chokepoint lets the road segments around it melt away even as you win the block

options.title: Bridge Around It
advantages: Lay a field crossing or detour over the ice to get around the block without a fight
Saves the column's strength for the outposts and denies the Hoarfrost the fight they set up
A detour the band did not expect can put the column behind them
disadvantages: Building a detour on rotting ice is slow, and the road-clock does not pause for it
The detour route may be exactly where the next block waits, or may simply not hold the weight
Time spent bridging is time an unreached outpost spends burning its last fuel
options.consequence: You refuse the band's fight and fight the road instead. The detour holds or it cracks, and the hours it costs come straight off the lives at the end of the route.

costs.resource: road-life clock spent building a detour over ice that may not hold it
costs.risk: the detour fails or leads to the next block, and you have spent your margin to arrive nowhere faster

options.title: Cut the Band's Cache
advantages: {NPC:intel-source} can point you to the Hoarfrost's fuel and ammunition cache off the road. Take it, and the block loses its staying power and the band loses its winter
Pulls the band off the chokepoint to defend the one thing it cannot live without
Completes the bonus objective at the same time
disadvantages: A raid off the road pulls a detachment away from a column that needs every machine moving forward
The cache report came by sled and is days old, so the band may have moved it
Splitting the force in front of a prepared block invites the block to become a trap
options.consequence: You go for the band's throat instead of its block. If it lands, the whole reach opens up. If it misses, the relief loses strength and time it does not have. The Hoarfrost stop blocking the road only when the road stops mattering to them.

costs.resource: a detachment and a slice of road-clock, gambled against a report that is days old
costs.risk: the cache is moved or guarded, the raid comes back empty, and the margin that would have reached an outpost is gone

entries.event: Alarm: the lead element's ice-scanning gear finds pressure-cracks opening across the road ahead a full day early. The thaw is running faster than the brief said. The road-clock is revised down on the spot.
A sled scout reports a Hoarfrost demolition party working a span at the next chokepoint north. It is not blown yet; the charges are being set for a later hour.
The southernmost outpost is reached or passed. Its fuel state confirms the consortium's estimate was too optimistic by days.
A warm front moves up the reach, speeding the melt on every open segment at once. The ice at the Narrows starts to turn brittle.
The Hoarfrost block springs at the chosen chokepoint, timed to the softening ice. The decision at the block can no longer wait.
Expected first-segment failure: the southern road starts closing behind the column. From here, every kilometer north is one that may not be driven back.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The road closes when the road closes, segment by segment, on the thaw's schedule and not the column's. The hard limit is the ice breaking up at the Narrows. Once the sound opens, everything north of it is stuck for the year and everything that did not get there is on its own. Whatever the column has delivered and whoever it has carried out by then is the whole run. The rest is a list the consortium reads next freeze, if it runs the road again at all.

opforSketch.composition: The Hoarfrost raider band, winter-adapted and road-wise: a reinforced company of cold-weather combat vehicles and hover units as the striking weight (this is the combined-arms core — armor and hovercraft that move on ice where 'Mechs sink and slow), 2-4 raider BattleMechs of mixed light-medium grade (Regular, a Veteran leader who has wintered here twice), demolition teams, and sled-mounted infantry. No DropShip presence on the reach — they live here. Behavioral breakpoint: the band breaks off any engagement that threatens its fuel cache and will trade a sprung block to draw the column toward it.
opforSketch.behavior: Patient and parasitic. The Hoarfrost do not seek decisive battle; they time blocks and ambushes to the melt for maximum permanence, harass the column to slow it, and let the road do the killing. They fight hardest only over their cache and their cold-weather mobility — the two things that let them own a reach nobody else can hold in winter. Pressed, they scatter onto the ice and re-form, because the season is their ally and the thaw is everyone else's enemy.

forks.name: OPERATION SPRING THAW
forks.trigger: Four or five outposts relieved and the column home, with the Hoarfrost's hold broken.
forks.consequence: The consortium contracts the unit to hold the reach through the open season the band used to own — a summer garrison over thawed ground and open water, mapping the route, fortifying the chokepoints, and making sure next winter's run is a delivery and not a siege.

forks.name: OPERATION LAST FREEZE
forks.trigger: The road closes with outposts unreached, or the column is stranded north of a failed crossing.
forks.consequence: Whatever the thaw cut off is cut off until next winter — including, perhaps, the relief force itself. The follow-on is a desperate over-water lift improvised against open season: chartered VTOLs and amphibians against the Hoarfrost, to reach people the ice road already failed.

forks.name: OPERATION DROWNED ROAD
forks.trigger: The Hoarfrost take or destroy a relieved outpost's delivered fuel, or seize a stranded hauler intact.
forks.consequence: The band gets exactly what it winters on — fuel and machines straight off the relief column — and grows from a parasite into a force that can contest the reach outright. The consortium's next problem is not a hard winter but an enemy strong enough to take the smelter towns, and the unit's relief run becomes the reason it could.

storyElementSeed: At a refueling halt, a hauler driver chips a winter's worth of road ice off the bowser's valve so the fuel will flow, and listens to the sound under her boots change pitch from the hard crack of deep freeze to the wet groan of ice that is thinking about leaving. She finishes the fueling a little faster.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Relieve the outposts the road still allows, and bring the column home. The Commonwealth does not abandon its own miners lightly, but it will not drown a relief column in open water to reach them either. Save what the ice allows, and account honestly for the rest.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no reserve to cover losses on the ice. Machines that break through the ice, and haulers written off, are not insured this run. The consortium will pay you back slowly, if at all, so every machine on the Narrows is your own money under the water.
You have no engineers under contract. The consortium's mine crews build the detour under your cover. Add 1 day per detour, and accept that their gear is built for ore roads, not combat crossings.

title: OPERATION GLASS FRONTIER
skeleton: an expanding Clan assault force must take a defended world by the formal batchall it bid low to win the honor of, then hold the won ground as occupied territory it intends to govern, where the bid that secured the right to attack also fixed the force it may use and any reinforcement beyond the bid forfeits the honor the conquest exists to earn, so the crux is conquering and keeping with a deliberately insufficient force rather than overwhelming
inspiration: a frontier conquest that must garrison what it seizes with the same troops that seized it — the Roman limes advance where the conquering legion becomes the occupying one, antiquity
situation:
The Wolf Empire's frontier keeps expanding, and {WORLD} is the next stone in the wall. Your superior, {NPC:opfor-commander}, won the right to take this world the proper way, ordering it down to you through {NPC:employer-contact}. A batchall was cried to the defenders, and a bid was laid down to claim the assault for this Cluster over rival Wolf commanders who wanted it. The bid was aggressive. To earn the honor of the conquest, the force was cut to {BID_STARS} Stars and not one Point more. That is fewer machines than a cautious commander would bring, and that is exactly the point. A Wolf who needs a whole Galaxy to take a frontier world has not earned it. A Wolf who takes it with a bid this lean has.

You command the lead Trinary. The defenders are not Clan and do not fight by the Forms. The {TARGET_FACTION} garrison here is a Republic-remnant brigade gone feral in the Blackout, reinforced by hired Inner Sphere mercenaries. They answered the batchall with contempt, and they raise a problem the Forms do not cover: what happens when you still have to live on the ground you win. {WORLD} is not a raid. The Empire means to keep it: its foundries, its people, its place on the wall. The force that conquers it is the force that must then occupy it. Every machine spent taking the capital is a machine not guarding it next month, and there are no replacements that do not cost the honor of the bid.

The terrain problem is the foundry quarter of the capital, the prize that makes {WORLD} worth a bid at all. It is dense urban ground, the {DISTRICT} works: 4-to-8-story ferrocrete, streets 12 to 20 meters wide, and the smelters and forge-halls the Empire wants taken whole and running. The defenders have fortified it exactly because the Clans cannot simply flatten what they came to own. Level the quarter with fire and you win the battle but lose the reason for it. Taking it intact means fighting through it at close range, in a city, against an enemy who knows the Wolves will not burn the thing they came to inherit.

Every sign says the defenders mean to force a choice on the Wolves: either a conquest so costly the lean bid cannot also garrison the result, or a foundry quarter so wrecked the conquest is hollow. {NPC:intel-source}'s assessment is blunt. The garrison cannot win. It does not need to. It needs only to make the won world impossible for the force that won it to govern.

objectives.primary: Take {WORLD}'s capital and foundry quarter under the terms of the batchall, using the bid force and no more, then hold the won ground as occupied territory.
objectives.secondary: Take the foundry quarter mostly intact. Keep the smelters, forge-halls, and skilled workers functioning, not smashed to rubble in the winning.
objectives.bonus: Secure the defeated so the occupation starts with a garrison the bid can actually support: surrendered mercenaries taken as bondsmen or paroled, and the population's submission won.

complications.name: The Bid Is the Limit
complications.text: Honor fixed the force at {BID_STARS} Stars. You can only add more by forfeiting the conquest's honor to a rival commander, which destroys the whole reason for the campaign. The force that lands is the force that finishes, win or lose.
complications.mechanicalEffect: No reinforcement is possible unless you forfeit the conquest to a rival at the campaign level. Every loss is permanent for the operation. The garrison you have after victory is the surviving bid force minus whatever the holding actions and the bonding take.

complications.name: The Prize Must Survive
complications.text: The foundry quarter is both the objective and the limit on how you can fight. Smash it and you win a battle but throw away the value the Empire bid to gain. The defenders fortified it knowing the Wolves dare not burn their own inheritance.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Heavy-weapon and area fire in the foundry quarter damages the secondary objective and lowers the world's value after the conquest. The defenders mass in the works to exploit the Clans' reluctance to fire. Clearing it intact means close fighting, which costs the bid force casualties.

complications.name: Ungovernable by Design
complications.text: The garrison fights to make the world impossible to hold, not to avoid losing. Every street they make the Wolves pay for is a street the occupation garrison cannot watch later. Every quarter wrecked in the taking is a quarter that breeds resistance after.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The defenders give up ground and accept their own losses to wear down the bid force and damage the prize as much as possible. Victory is graded not only on winning but on how much force and intact value you have left to hold the world afterward.

decisionPoints.name: The Form of the Assault
decisionPoints.context: The capital must fall and the foundry quarter must survive, both with a force deliberately bid too small. How the Trinary fights the city decides whether the Empire inherits a working world or garrisons a ruin with troops it cannot spare.

options.title: Honor Duels in the Streets
advantages: Fight by zellbrigen where the defenders allow it: single combats that spend the enemy's best while sparing both the works and the bid force
The cleanest path to an intact foundry quarter, because duels do not level forge-halls
Warriors you can take as bondsmen and an honorable conquest, the richest possible start to an occupation
disadvantages: The {TARGET_FACTION} garrison does not fight by the Forms and will gang up on any Wolf who fights one-on-one
Honoring a code the enemy ignores bleeds the bid force against an enemy who spends nothing on honor
A Trinary fighting duels in a city it must clear moves slowly while the defenders set the next trap
options.consequence: The Wolves fight the war they wish they were in. The foundry survives and the conquest is honorable, if the bid force survives an enemy who answers ritual with massed autocannon fire. The code that makes the victory worth having may be the thing that prevents it.

costs.resource: the bid force's strength, lost honoring a code the enemy exploits while giving nothing back
costs.risk: duels against an enemy who swarms the duelist bleed the lean force faster than the city can be cleared

options.title: Massed and Quick
advantages: Drop the duel where the enemy drops it and fight as one concentrated fist, taking the capital fast before losses grind the lean bid down
Speed limits the defenders' chances to wreck the works and the streets
Saves the bid force by ending the battle before the city can consume it
disadvantages: Massed Clan fire in a foundry quarter is exactly the collateral damage the defenders want, so speed risks the prize
Fighting unlike Wolves, even when justified, costs the honor the bid was meant to earn
A fast assault that wrecks the works wins {WORLD} and loses the reason the Empire wanted it
options.consequence: The Trinary trades the Form for the bid force's survival and bets the prize on its own fire discipline. The capital falls fast, and the foundry quarter is intact or it is not, and the difference is every round fired indoors.

costs.resource: the foundry quarter's intact value and some of the conquest's honor, spent to gain speed
costs.risk: massed fire in the works hands the defenders their victory: a won world not worth the winning

options.title: Turn the Mercenaries First
advantages: The hired Inner Sphere troops fight for pay, not for {WORLD}. A batchall aimed at them, or terms offered mid-battle, may turn or remove them before you even reach the capital
Stripping the mercenaries from the garrison cuts the defense in half and leaves only the feral remnant
Bondsmen and paroled mercenaries become the manpower the occupation badly needs
disadvantages: Bargaining with mercenaries during the conquest costs time the bid force could spend winning, and that time lets the defenders dig in deeper
The Republic remnant may kill the deal-makers or fight harder to stop the defection
Turned mercenaries are troops the Wolves must now watch too: bondsmen of unproven loyalty inside the won city
options.consequence: The Trinary attacks the enemy's wallet before its line. If the mercenaries fold, the conquest gets cheaper and the occupation gets its garrison. If they do not, the Wolves have shown their weakness: a bid too lean to win without a deal.

costs.resource: time, and the look of strength, because a bid force that bargains has admitted it cannot simply take the world
costs.risk: the offer fails in public and the defenders learn the lean bid is leaning on a deal it could not close

decisionPoints.name: The Garrison Question
decisionPoints.context: The capital is falling, and the aftermath is already here. The same Stars that took the city must hold the city, the foundry, the population, and the frontier behind it. There is no reinforcement that does not cost the conquest's honor. You must split the force between finishing the fight and surviving the peace.

options.title: Commit Everything to the Win
advantages: Throw the whole bid force at the foundry quarter and take it fast and whole, then settle the garrison question once the city is surely won
Maximum combat power at the key point means the fewest total losses to take the prize intact
A clean, fast conquest leaves the most force for the occupation precisely by holding none back
disadvantages: Nothing watches the won quarters, the prisoners, or the frontier road while the whole force fights forward
A defender counterattack into the cleared rear, or a prisoner uprising, hits an empty occupation
If the win costs more than expected, the occupation starts with whatever crawls out of the foundry
options.consequence: The Trinary bets that the fastest win is the cheapest garrison. That holds if the city falls clean, and fails if the defenders have one more trick behind the line, and the bid leaves no room to be wrong.

costs.resource: all rear security: the won ground, the prisoners, and the frontier left unwatched until the city is taken
costs.risk: a counterattack or uprising in the unguarded rear turns a won city into a two-front fight the lean force cannot hold

options.title: Peel Off a Holding Star Early
advantages: Pull a Star aside to garrison the won ground, secure the bondsmen, and screen the frontier while the assault continues, so the occupation starts before the battle ends
No empty rear for the defenders to exploit; the conquest and the holding run at the same time
The bondsmen and the population are held from the first hour, the strongest start for governing the world
disadvantages: A Star pulled aside is a Star not in the foundry fight, so the assault slows and the prize stays in the defenders' hands longer
A slower assault is a bloodier one against an enemy fighting to wear you down
The detached Star may face the very counterattack it was posted to prevent, and face it alone
options.consequence: The Trinary fights the conquest and the occupation at once with a force too small for either. The won ground stays held and the foundry takes longer to win, and the thin bid is felt in both halves at the same time.

costs.resource: a Star's combat weight, pulled from the assault to start the occupation early
costs.risk: a slowed assault bleeds more in the foundry while the holding Star fights its own battle in the rear

options.title: Govern Through the Defeated
advantages: Plan from the first hour to hold the world with its own people and the bondsmen rather than the bid force: keep the magistrates, parole the mercenaries to police their own, and restart the works under Wolf oversight
Frees the entire bid force to stay a field force, not a garrison
The only way a lean bid can actually keep a frontier world for the long term
disadvantages: A government built from the just-defeated is fragile, slow to set up, and open to betrayal at every level
It needs the foundry quarter and its skilled workers taken nearly intact, so failing the assault kills the occupation plan too
The first test of the arrangement is a resistance the Wolves cannot be everywhere at once to put down
options.consequence: The Trinary wins the world by planning to be ruled for, not to rule directly. It is the boldest answer to the bid's limit and the most exposed: the occupation rests on the loyalty of people the Wolves conquered last week, and conquered loyalty is only rented.

costs.resource: a permanent reliance on the defeated to hold a world the bid force cannot garrison alone
costs.risk: the government built from the conquered turns the first time the Wolves are not watching, and the lean force is all there is to answer it

entries.event: The batchall is acknowledged and refused with contempt. The bid force lands at the agreed ground and the Trinary forms up to advance on the capital. The honor of the conquest is now tied to this force and no other.
First contact at the capital's outer industrial ring. The {TARGET_FACTION} garrison refuses single combat and fights with massed fire. The kind of war the defenders intend is now clear.
The Trinary reaches the edge of the foundry quarter. Defenders are dug into the forge-halls, using the works as both fortress and hostage. The fire-discipline problem is now immediate.
The mercenary element is spotted holding its own sector, fighting for pay rather than for the world. This is the seam in the defense, and the window to work it is open.

Expected turning point of the first phase: the foundry quarter is fought over street by street, the bid force is taking the losses the defenders counted on, and the rear thins as machines are drawn forward.
Defender last-stand or counterattack window. The garrison spends its last strength either holding the works to the end or striking the Wolf rear, depending on how the Trinary set up.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The conquest is limited not by a clock but by the bid. When the bid force is spent, it is spent, and there is no more without forfeiting the honor the whole campaign exists to win. The hard limit is the moment the surviving force can no longer both finish the fight and hold the result. Past that point, the Wolves either take a ruin they cannot garrison or break off a conquest they cannot finish, and the defenders, who never needed to win, will have made the won world impossible for the hand that won it to govern.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} garrison: a Republic-remnant brigade core gone independent in the Blackout — 1-2 BattleMech battalions of mixed Inner Sphere designs (Regular, dug into the foundry quarter and fighting from prepared urban positions), reinforced by a hired mercenary 'Mech battalion (Regular-to-Veteran, holding a distinct sector for pay). This is a MECH_ONLY action by the terms of the batchall — the bid and the defenders' answer are 'Mech-on-'Mech, the Clan way, however little the defenders honor the rest of the Forms. Behavioral breakpoint: the feral remnant fights to the destruction of the prize; the mercenary element breaks off or defects when the pay no longer justifies the dying.
opforSketch.behavior: The defenders fight an attrition-and-collateral war, not a battle for victory. They refuse zellbrigen, mass fire on isolated Wolves, fortify the works to exploit Clan reluctance to burn the prize, and trade their own losses and the city's ruin for maximum cost to the lean bid force. Their aim is not to hold {WORLD} but to ensure that whoever takes it cannot keep it. The mercenaries fight a colder calculation entirely, and that seam is the Trinary's best lever.

forks.name: OPERATION HELD WALL
forks.trigger: The capital and foundry taken intact with the bid force, the defeated bound, and a sustainable occupation in place.
forks.consequence: {WORLD} becomes a stone in the wall that holds. The Trinary stands as its garrison while the frontier advances past it — and the first test comes from outside: a rival power, Jade Falcon or House, probing the newly won world to see whether the lean force that took it can also keep it.

forks.name: OPERATION HOLLOW CROWN
forks.trigger: The bid force is broken, the foundry wrecked, or the conquest stalls short of holdable victory.
forks.consequence: The defenders achieve exactly what they intended: a Wolf force too spent to keep what it bled for. Command must choose between forfeiting the conquest's honor to bring in a fresh Galaxy or abandoning a half-taken world — and either choice is a defeat the Cluster's rivals will remember.

forks.name: OPERATION BOUGHT LINE
forks.trigger: The mercenaries are turned but their loyalty proves false, or the conquered occupation structure rises early.
forks.consequence: The garrison the Wolves built from the defeated turns inside the won city. The Trinary, dispersed to hold a frontier world with borrowed manpower, must now suppress a rising among the very people it was relying on to govern — a battle for ground it already conquered once.

storyElementSeed: In a captured forge-hall, the smelters still hold their heat — the defenders did not have time to cool them, or did not dare. A Wolf warrior, out of her cockpit, lays a gauntleted hand near the crucible glow and does not give the order to fire that would crack the hall around it. The thing is worth more whole. So, she is beginning to understand, is the world.

clan.objectives.primary: Take this world with the bid we cried, and hold it with our own hands. A conquest that needs more than it bid is no conquest. A world won and then lost to its own people is worse than one never claimed. We take {WORLD} lean and we keep it, or we have earned nothing.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no fund to buy out a mercenary contract. The offer has to be made in bondage and honor alone, which is a harder sell to soldiers who came for pay, and slower to close, if it closes at all.

No administrators landed with the bid. The government has to be run by the Trinary's own warriors standing watch over magistrates. Accept a permanent drain on command attention, and accept that warriors make poor governors.

title: OPERATION SETTLED ACCOUNTS
skeleton: an occupation force newly installed over a reconquered world must hold a restive capital through the transition while the deposed regime's stay-behind apparatus and a rival claimant both work the population, where heavy suppression manufactures the rising it fears and visible restraint is read as weakness to be tested, so the crux is holding a city by judgment of force across an occupation rather than by winning a battle
inspiration: the hard first months of a reconquest occupation — holding a hostile capital through transition while an underground and a rival both contest it, mid-20th century
situation:
{WORLD} came back to the Combine the way most things do in the Blackout: taken by force, not handed over. The {EMPLOYER}'s regulars took the world from a Republic-remnant administration in a campaign that is already over. The field army has moved on to the next world on the list, and what it left behind is your unit, an occupation contract, and a capital that has not made up its mind yet. {NPC:employer-contact}, the {EMPLOYER}'s appointed planetary overseer, wants the city district of {DISTRICT} kept quiet through the {TRANSITION_DAYS}-day handover to civilian government. Quiet is the word in the contract. Nobody believes in it.

The old administration did not all leave. {NPC:intel-source} reports a Republic-loyalist underground still working in the capital: weapon caches, cells, and a core of former security officers who know the city's weak points because they built them. They have not risen yet. They are waiting to see if the occupation gives them a reason, and the reason they want most is a heavy-handed sweep that turns a sullen population into recruits. Their early work is patient: an arrest that becomes a funeral, a seizure that becomes a grievance, a checkpoint incident filmed and passed hand to hand. They are not trying to beat the garrison. They are trying to make the garrison turn on the city.

There is a third player. A rival claimant, a {TARGET_FACTION} interest two jumps away that wanted {WORLD} for itself, is working the same population from the other side. It funds agitators and spreads the promise that a different flag would rule more gently. The two pressures do not coordinate, and they do not need to. Every time the garrison overreacts, both of them gain. Note that this intelligence is 8 to 20 days old, more reliable on the underground than on the rival's reach.

The terrain problem is the old quarter, the capital's dense pre-Republic core, the {DISTRICT} warrens: 3-to-6-story masonry, streets too narrow for two vehicles side by side, and a thousand inner courtyards and connecting cellars no occupation map has ever fully shown. This is where the people are packed tightest, where the underground is rooted, and where any use of force is watched from a hundred windows. A 'Mech rules the wide boulevards but is blind and hated in the warrens. The garrison can hold the city's skeleton with armor. The city's heart is held by good judgment or not at all.

objectives.primary: Hold the capital through the {TRANSITION_DAYS}-day handover to civilian government: no general uprising, no district lost to the underground, and the handover done with the city still governable.
objectives.secondary: Wear down the Republic underground by seizing caches, rolling up cells, and taking out the former-officer core, all without the mass-arrest campaign that would feed it.
objectives.bonus: Expose the rival claimant to the population. Show proof of foreign meddling that turns the city's anger outward instead of at the occupier.

complications.name: Force Makes the Enemy
complications.text: The underground's whole plan is to recruit off the occupation's mistakes. Every heavy sweep, group punishment, or show of force in the warrens turns neutral citizens into informants for the other side.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A city-mood track reacts to how the garrison acts. Heavy-handed actions lower it and boost the underground's recruiting and intelligence. Visible restraint and careful, targeted action hold it steady or raise it. The city mood controls which cells you can find and whether an uprising spreads.

complications.name: The Patient Underground
complications.text: The former-officer core knows the city because they used to police it. They wait, provoke, and film, raising the cost of every garrison act, and they will not commit to an uprising until the occupation has built one for them.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The underground runs provocation events meant to draw an overreaction, not to cause direct harm. A provocation that succeeds in drawing a heavy response advances an uprising clock; restraint stalls it. You can only fully find the underground through intelligence, which the city mood controls, not through sweeps.

complications.name: Two Sides, One Result
complications.text: The Republic underground and the rival claimant pull the population in opposite directions, and both gain from the same garrison mistakes. The garrison fights on two fronts that share one weakness: its own temper.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Rival-claimant agitation events add to the underground's provocations on the city-mood track. The two do not coordinate and can be turned against each other. Exposing one to the population can discredit the other, if the garrison is trusted enough to be believed.

decisionPoints.name: The Posture of the Occupation
decisionPoints.context: The handover runs {TRANSITION_DAYS} days through a city that has not yet picked a side. The garrison's standing posture, set now and read by everyone, decides whether the underground gets the overreaction it needs and whether the population settles down or hardens.

options.title: Mailed Fist
advantages: Curfew, checkpoints, and a fast, firm response to any incident deny the underground freedom to move and leave no doubt who holds the city
Visible strength scares opportunists and fence-sitters off joining anything
The fastest way to shut down an active cell once you find it
disadvantages: A heavy posture is the underground's best recruiter, because every hard act in the warrens is filmed, mourned, and avenged
Group punishment creates the broad grievance the former-officer core cannot create on its own
A city held by fear is held only while the fist is everywhere, and the garrison cannot be everywhere
options.consequence: You hold the city by pressure and pay for it in the city's mood. The underground is hunted hard and fed harder. The handover goes on under a lid the underground is patiently working to blow off.

costs.resource: the city's mood, spent steadily, because every heavy act pushes neutrals toward the underground
costs.risk: the crackdown creates the very uprising it is trying to prevent, and the handover ends in the explosion the posture invited

options.title: Open Hand
advantages: A light footprint, targeted force, and visible rebuilding and restraint deny the underground the overreaction its whole plan depends on
Holds and improves the city mood, which opens the intelligence that finds cells without sweeps
A population that is not being punished has less reason to shelter the people you are hunting
disadvantages: Both the underground and the rival read restraint as weakness to test, and the tests come early and often
Targeted action is slow, and a cell left alone a week longer is a cell that strikes
The overseer wants quiet, and in the short term an open hand looks exactly like a garrison that has lost its grip
options.consequence: You hold the city by legitimacy and bet that a population left its dignity will not rise for the people who would take it. It is the lasting answer and the slow one, and every probe you absorb without overreacting is a temptation resisted at a visible cost.

costs.resource: the look of control: restraint that reads as weakness until it is proven right
costs.risk: the underground and the rival push their probes harder precisely because restraint invites it, and one probe too many becomes a real loss

options.title: Recruit the Old Police
advantages: The Republic administration's own street police know the city and the former-officer core. Turned or paroled into the occupation, they can police the warrens the garrison cannot
A local face on enforcement cuts in half the foreign-occupier grievance the rival is selling
Their knowledge is the fastest way into the underground, because they worked beside half of it
disadvantages: The old police are full of the underground's own people, so recruiting them may invite the enemy right inside your own structure
A local force enforcing for the occupier is a traitor to the loyalists and a target to every side
Their loyalty is rented, and the rent comes due at the worst possible moment
options.consequence: You govern the city through the city's own hands and accept that some of those hands belong to the enemy. It is the only posture that can hold the warrens cheaply, and the one most likely to be holding a knife.

costs.resource: the trustworthiness of your own enforcement, opened up to infiltration by the underground it is policing
costs.risk: the recruited police are turned, or already turned, and your grip on the warrens becomes the underground's grip on you

decisionPoints.name: The Funeral
decisionPoints.context: A checkpoint goes wrong: a fleeing car, a nervous gunner, a dead civilian who may or may not have been underground. By morning a funeral is forming in the old quarter, thousands strong, and the underground is steering it toward the garrison's main boulevard post. This is the provocation they have been building toward, and how the garrison responds is the whole game.

options.title: Lock Down the Quarter
advantages: Seal the warrens, redirect the procession, and deny the underground its planned confrontation before it can catch fire
Keeps a huge crowd from reaching the garrison's positions, where a second incident becomes a massacre
Firm control of the most dangerous hours
disadvantages: Sealing off a funeral is the image the underground wants even more than the funeral itself: an occupier that fears the grieving
A locked-down quarter is a provocation in itself, and the crowd may push a cordon that then has to fire or fold
The city mood collapses whether or not a shot is fired
options.consequence: You smother the planned confrontation and hand the underground a different picture instead: the occupier who would not let a city bury its dead. The immediate danger passes and the longer war gets worse.

costs.resource: the city's mood, spent heavily to deny one confrontation by creating a different grievance
costs.risk: a cordon pushed by the crowd has to open fire or break, and either outcome is the underground's victory

options.title: Stand Aside and Account
advantages: Let the funeral proceed, pull the garrison back from its route, and openly launch an honest inquiry into the checkpoint death, meeting the provocation with accountability
Denies the underground its confrontation by refusing to be the enemy it needs
An occupier seen to hold its own people to account is the rival's nightmare and a surprise to the population
disadvantages: Standing aside gives up the streets for a day and looks, to the overseer and the opportunists, like an occupation that has lost the city
An inquiry that finds the garrison at fault is a real cost paid in front of everyone
If the underground turns the peaceful procession into a riot anyway, the garrison has handed over the ground to organize one
options.consequence: You refuse the trap by taking the blow in public. The funeral becomes a funeral, the inquiry becomes a test of whether the occupier means it, and the underground is left holding a confrontation that never happened.

costs.resource: the look of control, and possibly a ruling of fault against your own troops, paid in reputation
costs.risk: the procession turns into a riot anyway and the garrison has to retake streets it chose to give up, now full of organized anger

options.title: Turn the Funeral on the Rival
advantages: {NPC:intel-source} can prove the agitators steering the procession are the rival claimant's paid hands, not loyalist mourners. Show it, and the crowd's anger has somewhere else to go
Splits the underground from the rival, and the mourners from both
Turns a provocation into the bonus objective: foreign meddling exposed with the whole city watching
disadvantages: The proof has to convince a hostile crowd on the spot, which is a hard sell from an occupier nobody trusts yet
If the crowd reads the exposure as a frame-up, the garrison has added a lie to a killing
Acting on the procession at all, even with the truth, risks the second incident that ends everything
options.consequence: You fight the provocation with information instead of force, betting your thin credibility on a crowd believing the occupier over the agitator. If it lands, the city's anger turns outward. If it does not, you have spoken into a riot and been disbelieved.

costs.resource: the garrison's thin credibility, bet on a hostile crowd taking the occupier's word over a mourner's
costs.risk: the crowd reads it as a frame, and the killing plus the 'lie' together hand the underground its general uprising

entries.event: Alarm: a coordinated night of provocations across the old quarter at once, with three checkpoint confrontations, a cache fire, and a flood of leaflets. The underground is testing the garrison's posture and reflexes in one stroke.
Garrison reaction units move to the flashpoints. The warrens fill with onlookers, and the rival's agitators start steering the crowds toward the garrison's strongpoints.
First serious clash between a crowd and a cordon at a boulevard post. The decision the garrison's posture has been building toward arrives in the open, on camera.
If the response was heavy, the uprising clock jumps and the warrens start barricading. If it was restrained, the crowds thin and the underground's set-piece fizzles.
The night's handling sets the city's mood for the week. The mood moves up or down, and the underground plans its next move around it.
Handover to civilian government: the end point of the contract. Whatever state the city is in that morning is the state the garrison delivers and is judged on.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The handover comes on day {TRANSITION_DAYS}, and the city passes to civilian government in whatever condition the occupation has left it. The hard limit is a general uprising: if the underground, fed by the garrison's own posture, tips the population over before the handover, the handover fails and the contract with it. Quiet was always the wrong word. The garrison's job is to reach the handover with a city that can be governed, by careful use of force across the occupation, against two players working to make it ungovernable and a clock that does not extend.

opforSketch.composition: No conventional field army — the war here is occupation. Threats: the Republic stay-behind apparatus (former security cadre and cells, small arms, demolitions, intimate city knowledge — Green as soldiers, Veteran at subversion); rival-claimant agitators (unarmed influence operators, deniable funding); and, on the campaign layer, two hard military contingencies if the city tips — an apparatus arms cache that fields IndustrialMech conversions and technicals (this is the combined-arms element: improvised armor and converted industrial 'Mechs rising in the warrens), and a rival-claimant relief probe of regular 'Mechs and armor if a general rising opens the door. Generator should keep the city game low-intensity and human until a rising converts it, then field the cache and probe forces.
opforSketch.behavior: The apparatus fights to be overreacted to: provoke, document, wait, and commit to armed rising only when the garrison has built the grievance for it. The rival agitates and probes, taking real military risk only if a rising cracks the occupation open. Neither needs to defeat the garrison in the field; both need the garrison to defeat itself in the warrens. The military forces appear only as the consequence of a posture gone wrong — the seasoning that becomes the meal if the city is mishandled.

forks.name: OPERATION CIVIL HAND
forks.trigger: The transition completes with the city governable, the apparatus degraded, and sentiment held.
forks.consequence: Civil administration takes the capital and the {EMPLOYER} extends the unit's contract to the second city on the world — a fresh restive district, the apparatus's surviving cells displaced into it, and a population that has heard how the capital was handled and will judge the garrison against that reputation from day one.

forks.name: OPERATION GENERAL RISING
forks.trigger: The apparatus tips the population into a general rising before the handover.
forks.consequence: The warrens go up: barricades, the arms cache fielded, the rival probing the chaos from outside. The unit fights a city it was sent to hold, the field army is a jump away and not coming back soon, and the transition is replaced by a counter-insurgency the contract never priced.

forks.name: OPERATION TURNED KEY
forks.trigger: The co-opted local police are revealed as apparatus-infiltrated, or the rival claimant turns a garrison error into open intervention.
forks.consequence: The occupation's own enforcement structure becomes a weapon against it — the warrens held by police who answer to the underground, or a rival contingent landed on the pretext of the garrison's misrule. The unit must now retake its own occupation from inside, with the population watching to see which occupier is worse.

storyElementSeed: A garrison sergeant on a warrens patrol stops to let an old woman pass with her water cans and, without thinking, takes one and carries it to her door. Three windows above, a man notes it down — not the lapse in security, but the courtesy. He is not sure yet which column it goes in.

is-kurita.objectives.primary: Hold the capital to the handover with both honor and order intact. A world reconquered is a world that must be ruled, not just beaten. The Dragon does not inherit ash and call it a province. Reach the handover with a city that bows because it is governed, not because it is afraid.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no funds for the rebuilding and relief that make restraint visible. An open hand with no bread behind it is just a thin garrison. Either add the cost of buying goodwill the budget cannot otherwise show, or accept restraint the city reads only as weakness.

You have no secure facility to vet recruits. The old police are taken on the overseer's say-so and a rushed interview. Accept a higher chance of infiltration and a longer wait before any of them can be trusted alone in the warrens.

title: OPERATION DRY MOUNTAIN
skeleton: a garrison must hold a fortified water-and-aquifer works that supplies a whole region against a besieger who can win simply by keeping the works shut off long enough, where the defenders' own demand for water is the clock and the besieger trades casualties for a siege whose passage of time is its real weapon, so the crux is enduring a thirst the garrison cannot resupply rather than repelling an assault
inspiration: the desert fortress siege where the well is the prize and the clock — Masada's cisterns and the water-starved hill forts of arid frontiers, antiquity
situation:
On {WORLD}, water is power. The {DISTRICT} aquifer works, which is deep wells, pumping halls, and the fortified ridge that holds them, supplies every settlement and farm on the dry plateau below, {DEPENDENT_POP} people with no other source within a week's travel. Whoever holds the works holds the region, and everyone on {WORLD} has always known it, which is why the works were built as a fortress. Your employer is {EMPLOYER}, the plateau settlements' water compact, and your contact is {NPC:employer-contact}. They hold the works and want you to keep holding them, because a besieger has come who understands the stakes exactly.

The besieger is a regional warlord, a Blackout strongman who has bolted a Republic-remnant battalion onto local levies and means to own the plateau by owning its water. {NPC:intel-source} puts the force at a reinforced battalion: a 'Mech company, armor, and the engineers and infantry to lay siege to a ridge. Note that this report is 4 to 11 days old. The warlord has not thrown himself at the walls and will not need to. His plan is clear from how he deploys: surround the works, cut the water mains where they cross the open ground below the ridge, and wait. A fortress that holds the region's water cannot drink it if the besieger has shut the pumps and cut the mains. The garrison's own reservoirs on the ridge will run dry. The clock is not the besieger's patience. The clock is the garrison's thirst.

The terrain problem is the ridge and the open ground below it. The works sit on a steep escarpment, sheer on three sides, with one fortified approach ramp and prepared positions with long fields of fire over the desert flat. It is a strong place to hold and a death trap to be besieged in. The water mains and intake galleries run down off the ridge onto that open flat, where the enemy can cut them and the garrison cannot reach them without leaving the walls. The escarpment that makes the works impossible to storm also leaves them dependent on equipment outside the wire, in the besieger's hands.

The garrison: the works' own security company, the compact's militia, and your unit. On the ridge: {RESERVOIR_DAYS} days of stored water at full ration for the garrison and the refugees already crowding up from the plateau, less with every day the warlord keeps the pumps off. The besieger has water. The besieger has time. The besieger has read the same water gauge the garrison reads. He is not trying to take the works. He is trying to make them thirsty enough to open the gate.

objectives.primary: Hold the aquifer works through the siege. Keep the wells, pumping halls, and ridge in the compact's hands, and do not surrender the region's water to the warlord.
objectives.secondary: Keep the garrison and the sheltering refugees supplied with water. Restore or protect enough of the pumping and intake equipment to make the ridge's water last past the besieger's patience.
objectives.bonus: Break the siege at its source. Beat the warlord's field force or split his coalition of levies, so the works are not just held but freed.

complications.name: The Water Gauge
complications.text: The ridge holds {RESERVOIR_DAYS} days of water at full ration, and every day the besieger keeps the pumps off draws it down. Refugees crowding up from the plateau drink from the same supply. The besieger tracks it as closely as the garrison does.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A water-days clock counts down each day the pumping equipment stays cut. Refugees speed it up; rationing or restoring the intake slows it. At low water the garrison takes combat and morale penalties. At zero the works must surrender, sortie out, or die of thirst, no matter how strong the walls are.

complications.name: The Pumps Are Outside the Wire
complications.text: The pumps, mains, and intake galleries that make the works valuable run down off the escarpment into open ground the besieger controls. The fortress cannot defend its own water supply without leaving the fortress.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Restoring or protecting the water equipment means sorties off the ridge into the besieger's siege lines. Each sortie is an exposed combined-arms fight in the open. The besieger fights for the equipment precisely because the garrison has to come out to reach it.

complications.name: Time Is the Weapon
complications.text: The warlord wins by waiting. He will spend casualties only to keep the pumps cut and the garrison penned in. He will not storm a fortress he can dry out instead. His patience is his artillery.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The besieger prefers surrounding the ridge, denying the water equipment, and running down the water clock over any assault. He attacks directly only to beat back a sortie or to hit a garrison already weak from thirst. The siege is graded on the water clock, not on attacks repelled.

decisionPoints.name: The Water Problem
decisionPoints.context: The pumps are off, the mains are cut, and the gauge is falling. The garrison can wait it out, fight for its water supply in the open, or shrink the problem by cutting who drinks. Each answer spends something the siege will demand again later.

options.title: Ration and Wait
advantages: Cut water use to the bone and stretch the ridge's supply far past what the besieger expects, outlasting the patience the warlord is counting on
No sorties, no exposure: the garrison stays behind the walls where it is strongest
Buys time for relief, for the levies to tire, or for the bonus play to develop
disadvantages: A rationed garrison is a weakened one, because thirst saps fighting power and morale before anything else
The refugees cannot be cut off entirely without a reckoning the compact will not forgive
Waiting is a bet that something changes before the gauge hits zero, and nothing may
options.consequence: You meet the besieger's clock with discipline and bet your thirst outlasts his patience. It is the strongest defensive posture and the slowest death if no relief or breakthrough comes: a contest of who blinks first, measured in canteens.

costs.resource: the garrison's fighting condition, traded away day by day as the ration tightens
costs.risk: waiting with no relief is just a slower surrender, and a thirst-weakened garrison may be too weak to sortie or hold when the moment finally comes

options.title: Sortie for the Pumps
advantages: Strike down off the ridge to retake and restart a pumping station or repair a cut main, refilling the gauge and wrecking the besieger's whole plan
An active defense seizes the initiative the warlord's patience gives up
A working pump turns the water clock from the garrison's enemy into its ally
disadvantages: A sortie leaves the escarpment's cover for open ground the besieger has prepared exactly for this
The warlord wants the garrison to come out; the pumps are bait as much as a lifeline
A failed sortie costs irreplaceable machines and the water it went to win
