options.consequence: You fight for your own water supply in the one place you are weakest. A won sortie buys water and pride. A lost one gives the besieger the attrition his patience could not, and leaves the gauge falling toward a garrison that is now smaller.

costs.resource: the safety of the walls, left behind for open ground the besieger has already ranged
costs.risk: the pumps are bait, and a sortie caught in the open trades the garrison's strength for water it may not even secure

options.title: Send the Refugees Down
advantages: Evacuate the refugees off the ridge under a truce or by night, removing the biggest drain on the gauge
A garrison drinking for its soldiers alone holds far longer on the same water
Frees the defense from protecting a crowd it cannot also supply with water
disadvantages: Sending plateau civilians into the besieger's lines hands them to the warlord who controls the only other water, giving up the very people the works exist to serve
The compact may forbid it outright, since the works are held for those people
The besieger may use a refugee column as cover, as hostages, or as a way into the gate
options.consequence: You save your water by giving up your reason for being there. The gauge holds longer and the works become a fortress defending only itself, not the region, and the warlord gains the population's dependence the moment they walk into his arms.

costs.resource: the refugees, and with them the works' whole purpose, handed down to the besieger to save the garrison's ration
costs.risk: the besieger uses the evacuation as a hostage lever or a breach, and the garrison has given the warlord both the people and an opening

decisionPoints.name: The Warlord's Coalition
decisionPoints.context: The besieging force is not one army but a core battalion stiffened with local levies who fight for the warlord's promises, not his cause. {NPC:intel-source} sees cracks: levies whose own settlements are on the thirsty plateau, who did not sign up to die in someone else's siege. The garrison can attack the besieger's walls, his will, or his alliances.

options.title: Outlast Him Whole
advantages: Treat the coalition as one and simply wait until the warlord's costs, in water, pay, casualties, and time, run past what he is willing to spend
No deals to be betrayed, no sortie to lose: the garrison's persistence is the whole strategy
A besieger who quits does so in front of his levies, and the coalition rots on its own
disadvantages: Outlasting him takes water the garrison may not have, and the warlord may have more patience than the gauge has days
Doing nothing to split the coalition lets it hold together longer than it would under pressure
It hands every bit of initiative to the besieger and bets everything on the reservoir
options.consequence: You answer the siege with pure endurance and let the besieger's own costs break his alliance. It works if the water lasts and the warlord's grip is weaker than it looks, and it is a long, dry gamble on both.

costs.resource: the water clock again, spent on the chance the besieger's coalition tires before the reservoir runs dry
costs.risk: the warlord's patience and his levies both outlast the gauge, and endurance alone delivers the works to thirst

options.title: Split the Levies
advantages: Reach the levy settlements with the truth: their own plateau is going thirsty under the siege their sons are manning, and the works' water is theirs too if the warlord is gone
Peeling levies off the coalition shrinks the besieging force without a shot
Makes the bonus objective live, because a split coalition is a broken siege
disadvantages: Bargaining with the besieger's own troops is slow, secret only until it is not, and may just harden the warlord's core
The levies may want the water for themselves, not for the compact, so splitting the siege could simply multiply the claimants
A failed approach tells the warlord exactly which levies to purge or watch
options.consequence: You attack the besieger's alliance instead of his line. If the levies break for home or for the compact, the siege thins to a core the works can outlast or sortie against. If they hold, the warlord learns his weak points are known and closes them.

costs.resource: time and secrecy, spent courting troops who may want the prize as much as the warlord does
costs.risk: the levies stay bought or take over the siege for themselves, and the garrison has spent its leverage to change the besieger's name, not end the siege

options.title: Break the Core by Sortie
advantages: Mass the garrison's mobile strength for one sortie aimed not at the pumps but at the warlord's command and the cohesion of his core battalion, cutting the head off the siege
A successful blow at the core scatters the levies, who were only ever following strength
The boldest path to actually freeing the works, not just holding them
disadvantages: Committing the garrison's strength to a sortie against the besieger's main body is the warlord's dream battle, on his ground
A failed strike spends the garrison's only mobile force and leaves the walls thinly held against thirst
Even a won sortie may not break a coalition that has the water and the time to re-form
options.consequence: You stake the siege on a single blow at the besieger's heart. Win it and the works are free. Lose it and the fortress holds only as long as its water and its few survivors last, against a besieger who now knows the garrison has spent its last card.

costs.resource: the garrison's entire mobile reserve, committed to one sortie against the besieger's main body
costs.risk: the strike fails, leaving the works defended by thirst and remnants, and the warlord with his core intact and his lesson learned

entries.event: Alarm: the besieger's engineers cut the last open water main below the ridge and seize the lower intake galleries. The pumps go off, and the water-days clock starts its real count.
The siege is complete. The warlord's battalion closes the ring around the escarpment, with prepared positions facing the approach ramp and the pump ground below. No assault; the siege settles in.
The refugee influx peaks as plateau settlements lose their piped water and flee uphill to the works. The gauge drains faster with every arrival at the gate.
First besieger probe of the approach ramp, testing the garrison's strength and alertness rather than committing. The warlord is taking the garrison's measure for the thirst to come.
Levy units are spotted holding the eastern siege line. This is the coalition's crack, and the window to work it is open and visible from the ridge.
The reservoir runs dry at full ration: the outer limit of the garrison's endurance with no pumps restored and no rationing. Every choice exists to push this date back or to make it matter less.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The siege is decided by the gauge, not the gate. The hard limit is the reservoir running dry. When the ridge's stored water runs out, the works must surrender, sortie out, or die of thirst behind walls that never fell. The warlord knows the date as well as the garrison does and has built his whole siege around outlasting it. Holding the works means making the water last past his patience, or breaking the siege before the gauge breaks the garrison, with a region's only water as the stake and a clock no wall can stop.

opforSketch.composition: A Blackout warlord's siege force: a Republic-remnant battalion core — a BattleMech company (Regular, with a Veteran command lance) and an armor company with combat engineers and infantry for the investment (this is the combined-arms weight — armor and engineers to cut mains, seize intakes, and invest the ridge) — stiffened by 1-2 companies of local levies (Green, mixed technicals and converted vehicles, uncertain commitment). No air to speak of; the besieger's strength is patience and position. Behavioral breakpoint: the core battalion presses only to keep the works invested and to crush sorties; the levies waver and may break if their own settlements or the siege's cost reach them.
opforSketch.behavior: The warlord besieges, he does not storm. His force invests the ridge, holds the cut infrastructure, repels sorties hard, and otherwise waits for thirst to do the work an assault would cost him. He trades casualties only to keep the pumps dark and the garrison penned. His weakness is his coalition: the levies fight for a winner, and a siege that drags, a settlement that thirsts, or a garrison that will not break tests their loyalty more than any sortie. He wins by time; he loses by patience running out before the reservoir does.

forks.name: OPERATION FULL CISTERN
forks.trigger: The works held with water secured and the siege broken or lifted.
forks.consequence: The compact, having kept its water and its world, contracts the unit to hold the works as the plateau's standing garrison and to bring the freed pumping network back to full supply — a quieter posting over the thing every power on {WORLD} will always want, with the warlord's survivors still out on the flat, thirsty and unforgiving.

forks.name: OPERATION DEAD WELL
forks.trigger: The reservoir runs dry and the works surrender, fall, or are abandoned to thirst.
forks.consequence: The warlord owns the region's water and therefore the region. The compact's survivors and whatever remains of the garrison fall back to the plateau settlements with a week's haul between them and dying of thirst — and the follow-on is a desperate fighting withdrawal across the dry flat, away from the well that beat them.

forks.name: OPERATION POISONED SPRING
forks.trigger: The besieger seizes a pumping station or intake intact, or the refugee evacuation is exploited into a breach.
forks.consequence: The warlord gets a hand on the water works themselves — a pump he can run for his own levies, or a foothold inside the wire through a column he turned. The garrison holds a fortress whose lifeline the enemy now partly controls, and must retake its own infrastructure from an enemy drinking the garrison's water.

storyElementSeed: At the ridge's main cistern, the works' chief engineer marks the day's water level with a scratch on the ferrocrete beside yesterday's and the day before's. The scratches march downward in a neat ladder. A militiaman filling his canteen looks at the ladder, then at his canteen, and tops it off a little less than full.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no depot of spare parts under contract. A retaken pump cannot be restarted without parts the works do not stock. Add a salvage-and-build delay before any restored station makes water, and accept that the besieger may re-cut it before it flows.

You have no reserve to cover a sortie's losses. Machines crippled in the strike cannot be replaced or repaired on the ridge. Every unit committed is your own capital, fighting in the open with no recovery line behind it.

title: OPERATION BROKEN ESCORT
skeleton: a relief force must fight a heavy ground convoy up a single jungle road through a layered ambush belt to reach a besieged factory town, where the road is the only route and the enemy fights not to stop the column but to bleed it thin enough that it arrives too weak to break the siege, so the crux is preserving enough of the relief through the gauntlet to still be a relief at the end of it
inspiration: the road-bound relief column fighting through successive ambushes to reach a cut-off garrison — the convoy battles of jungle and bush counter-insurgencies, mid-to-late 20th century
situation:
The {DISTRICT} factory town has been cut off for {SIEGE_WEEKS} weeks, and its survival now comes down to one road. {WORLD}'s interior is wet equatorial jungle, and the town, a Blackout-era refit works that still makes parts the region cannot get anywhere else, sits at the end of a single all-weather road through 140 kilometers of that jungle. The siege around the town is not strong enough to storm it, so the besieger's whole strategy is the road. Your employer is {EMPLOYER}, the regional March militia command, and your contact is {NPC:employer-contact}. They have assembled the relief: your unit, a militia mechanized battalion, and the heavy convoy the town actually needs, carrying ammunition, reactor parts, and the engineers to restart the town's defenses. The convoy is the mission. A relief force that arrives without it is just more mouths inside the wire.

The besieger has read this perfectly. {NPC:intel-source} reports the road seeded with a layered ambush belt: not one block but a string of prepared killing grounds along the route, each placed where the jungle pinches the road, each meant to cost the relief strength rather than stop it outright. Note that this report is 3 to 9 days old. The enemy does not expect to stop the column at any one ambush. The enemy expects the column to arrive, and to arrive so bled down by the gauntlet that it cannot break the siege when it gets there. The road does not have to beat the relief. It only has to whittle it down.

The terrain problem is the road itself and the jungle that owns it. The all-weather road is the only ground that carries heavy traffic for a hundred kilometers in any direction. Off it, the convoy's haulers and most of its armor simply bog down. The jungle presses right up to the edge, with sightlines of only tens of meters and ambush range point-blank, and the canopy hides movement and blinds air recon. Every kilometer is a possible killing ground, and the column cannot leave the road to avoid it. Move fast and the convoy is exposed to ambush without a screen. Move slow and the besieger has time to thicken the belt ahead and close it behind.

Inside the town, the garrison's own clock is running down. {SIEGE_WEEKS} weeks of fighting have left it with days of ammunition and reactor margin, and the besieger has started probing the perimeter hard now that the relief is on the road, trying to make the garrison spend its last reserves before help arrives. The relief must run the gauntlet fast enough to beat the garrison's collapse and intact enough to still be worth the running.

objectives.primary: Reach the besieged factory town with the relief convoy mostly intact and break the siege. Deliver the ammunition, reactor parts, and engineers, and restore the perimeter.
objectives.secondary: Get the relief force through the ambush belt in good shape. Arrive with enough combat power and enough of the convoy to actually break the siege, not just to reach it.
objectives.bonus: Keep the road open behind the column. Clear or hold the ambush belt so the town can be resupplied again, rather than relieved once and cut off again.

complications.name: The Road That Whittles You Down
complications.text: The ambush belt is built to thin the column, not to stop it. Each killing ground takes its toll and then lets the column pass, banking the besieger's win in the relief's casualties rather than in halting it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The route is a series of ambush events, each costing convoy vehicles and combat power rather than blocking the road outright. Arriving combat power is tracked as a running total, and the siege-break is graded on what reaches the town, not on whether the column arrives at all.

complications.name: The Road or Nothing
complications.text: The all-weather road is the only ground that carries the convoy. The jungle on either side bogs down haulers and armor, hides the enemy, and blinds the air recon that might spot the next ambush coming.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The convoy and most armor cannot leave the road. Going around an ambush off-road is slow, only partly possible, and risks bogging down. Air and ground recon ahead of the column is degraded by the canopy, so ambushes are spotted late and the belt's full depth is never fully known.

complications.name: The Garrison's Last Days
complications.text: The cut-off town has days of ammunition and reactor margin left, and the besieger is spending the garrison's reserves with probes timed to the relief's approach. Help that arrives late arrives at a town that has already fallen.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A garrison-survival clock runs down on its own and speeds up as the besieger probes. If it hits zero before the relief arrives, the perimeter falls and the mission changes from relief to recapture. The clock pushes the column to accept the casualties that come with speed.

decisionPoints.name: The Pace of the Column
decisionPoints.context: The garrison's clock says hurry; the ambush belt says do not. The column can run the gauntlet fast and take losses, advance carefully and fall behind, or split the difference and risk the worst of both. The pace you set now is the pace the besieger built his belt against.

options.title: Run the Gauntlet
advantages: Push hard and fast, take the ambushes as they come, and reach the town before the garrison's clock runs out
Speed denies the besieger time to thicken the belt ahead or close it behind
A fast column that takes its losses on the move is a column that arrives, and arriving in time is the whole point
disadvantages: Running through prepared killing grounds without a screen is exactly the casualty trade the besieger wants
A fast column cannot clear the belt behind it, so the road re-closes and the relief becomes a one-way trip
Haulers lost to point-blank ambush are convoy the town will not get, even if the force arrives
options.consequence: You trade blood for time and bet that what survives the run is still enough to break the siege. The garrison is reached before it falls, by a relief force the road has thinned out, arriving weak into a fight it must still win.

costs.resource: convoy and combat power, spent to the ambushes in exchange for the speed the garrison's clock demands
costs.risk: the gauntlet thins the relief below siege-breaking strength, and the column arrives in time only to fail at the wire

options.title: Advance by Bounds
advantages: Move carefully: screen ahead, clear each ambush before bringing up the convoy, and hold the cleared ground behind you
Keeps the relief's losses low and keeps the road open behind the column for later resupply
Arrives strong enough to break the siege for good, if it arrives
disadvantages: Careful is slow, and the garrison's clock does not wait for good tactics
Every hour spent clearing is an hour the besieger thickens the belt ahead
A column that arrives strong but late arrives to a town that has already fallen
options.consequence: You refuse the besieger's casualty trade and pay in time instead. It keeps the relief's strength and the road behind it, and bets that the garrison lasts the extra days the caution costs, a bet the besieger's probes are working to lose.

costs.resource: the garrison's survival clock, drawn down by the extra days a careful advance costs
costs.risk: the relief arrives intact and too late, breaking a siege around a perimeter that has already fallen

options.title: Split the Column
advantages: Send the combat power and the most critical cargo, ammunition and reactor parts, ahead fast as a light relief, with the heavy haulers and engineers following carefully behind
The town gets what it most needs soonest, and the fast element is small enough to take fewer ambushes
Gives the besieger two targets at two speeds to worry about
disadvantages: A split column is two weaker columns, each of which can be beaten on its own on a road built for ambush
The light element may break the siege but lack the engineers and parts to make the break hold
The heavy element behind is the slow, rich target the besieger most wants, with the screen gone on ahead
options.consequence: You gamble that speed and strength can be delivered in two doses instead of one. The town gets a fast lifeline and a slow follow-up, and the besieger gets two chances to whittle down a relief that divided itself on his road.

costs.resource: the column's unity: two elements at two speeds, each beatable alone on the ambush road
costs.risk: the besieger destroys the two elements one at a time, and the relief that split to do everything fast accomplishes neither half

decisionPoints.name: The Chokepoint at the River Crossing
decisionPoints.context: The belt's heaviest ambush sits where the road crosses a jungle river on a single bridge, the one point the column cannot go around and the besieger cannot let pass cheaply. The bridge is intact but covered by fire. Forcing it means fighting in the killing ground the whole belt was built around.

options.title: Force the Bridge
advantages: Smash across fast under covering fire, the only way through that keeps the column moving and the garrison's clock within reach
A forced crossing that works breaks the backbone of the ambush belt
Speed across a covered bridge cuts the time the column spends in the worst killing ground on the road
disadvantages: The bridge is the besieger's best-prepared position, so forcing it means paying his full price at his strongest point
A hauler or 'Mech knocked out on the bridge itself blocks the crossing for everyone behind
The crossing under fire is where the relief can be thinned out fastest of anywhere on the route
options.consequence: You pay the belt's biggest bill in one crossing. The backbone of the ambush breaks, or the bridge becomes a graveyard with the convoy stacked up behind it, and either way the garrison's clock keeps running while the river decides.

costs.resource: the relief's strength at its most concentrated, spent forcing the besieger's strongest prepared point
costs.risk: a wreck on the bridge blocks the crossing and pins the column in the killing ground the whole belt was built to create

options.title: Ford and Flank
advantages: Find a vehicle crossing up or downstream, send light elements over off the bridge, and take the ambush position from the side before pushing the convoy across
Undoes the prepared killing ground instead of paying for it head-on
Protects the convoy by clearing the crossing before committing it
disadvantages: A jungle-river crossing is slow, uncertain, and may not hold anything heavier than the light elements, so the convoy still uses the bridge
The flanking force is off the road and out of support, in jungle the besieger knows
Every hour spent finding and forcing a crossing is an hour off the garrison's clock
options.consequence: You refuse the head-on bill and spend time and risk to take the crossing cheaply. The flank turns the ambush, or it gets bogged down in the jungle, and the garrison's clock pays for the cleverness either way.

costs.resource: the garrison's survival clock, drawn down by the extra hours a ford-and-flank costs over a straight crossing
costs.risk: the crossing fails or the flank is caught in the jungle, and the column has lost time and a detachment to avoid a bridge it must still cross

options.title: Buy the Crossing
advantages: {NPC:intel-source} reports the besieger's force at the river crossing includes drafted local fighters with no love for the siege. A deal, a bribe, or a real threat may open the crossing without the full fight
Turns the belt's strongest point into its weakest if the local fighters step aside
Saves the relief's strength for the siege-break and keeps the road open behind
disadvantages: Bargaining at the killing ground is slow and leaves the column halted in the worst place on the road
The local fighters may take the bribe and shoot anyway, or the besieger's core may hold the bridge no matter what they do
A failed approach has spent time and shown the besieger exactly where the column means to cross
options.consequence: You try to talk your way through the besieger's best position. If the local fighters open the bridge, the belt's backbone breaks without a fight. If they do not, the column is halted at the killing ground with its plan given away and the garrison's clock still running.

costs.resource: time at the killing ground, and the money or leverage spent on fighters who may take both and fire anyway
costs.risk: the deal fails at the worst point on the road, and the column forces the bridge anyway, having lost time and surprise to the attempt

entries.event: Alarm: the column's lead screen takes fire at the first pinch in the road, 18 km out. It is a prepared ambush, sprung and then broken off as the screen deploys. The belt has shown itself, and the besieger's pattern is to bleed the column, not to hold it.

Air recon tries a sweep ahead. Canopy and ground fire give only a partial picture: at least three more ambush sites suspected ahead, depth unknown. The column advances into ground it cannot fully see.
Second ambush at a road pinch. The convoy takes its first hauler losses. Behind the column, the besieger starts re-seeding the cleared ground, so the road closes about as fast as it opens.
The garrison reports a major besieger probe against its perimeter. The enemy is spending the town's reserves to beat the relief's arrival. The garrison's clock jumps.
The column reaches the river crossing: the belt's heaviest prepared ambush, on the one bridge the convoy cannot go around. The crossing decision can no longer wait.
Expected arrival window at the town. By this point the relief is whatever the belt has left of it, and the siege-break is fought with that and no more.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Two clocks are running close together: the garrison's reserves and the relief's strength. The hard limit is the garrison's collapse. If the town's ammunition and reactor margin run out before the column arrives, the perimeter falls and the relief becomes a recapture against an enemy now holding the works. But arriving in time is only half the deadline. A column that beats the clock by running the belt may reach the wire too weak to break the siege. A column that saves its strength may reach it too late. The besieger built the road so that one of those two failures is always the easier trap to fall into. The relief must arrive both in time and intact, or it has not relieved anything.

opforSketch.composition: A besieging force fighting an economy-of-force siege and a road battle at once. On the road: a reinforced ambush element — light and medium BattleMechs (Regular, hit-and-run doctrine), ambush-sited armor and anti-'Mech infantry, demolition teams, and conscripted local fighters at the lighter positions (this is the combined-arms weight — ambush armor and infantry strung along the road, with the local levies as the soft seam). Around the town: the main besieging battalion — a 'Mech company and armor maintaining the investment and probing the perimeter. No air superiority; the canopy is the besieger's air defense. Behavioral breakpoint: ambush elements break contact rather than be decisively engaged, spending the relief's strength and preserving their own; the local fighters waver under pressure or a deal.
opforSketch.behavior: The besieger fights to subtract, not to stop. Road elements spring prepared ambushes, take their toll, and break off before the column can pin them, re-seeding the road behind to keep it cut. The aim is a relief bled too thin to matter, delivered to a garrison spent by timed probes. The main body around the town presses the perimeter to run down the garrison's clock as the relief approaches. The besieger's plan has no single decisive battle — it is a hundred kilometers of arithmetic, and its weakness is the conscripted fighters who were never paid to die for someone else's siege.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN ROAD
forks.trigger: The town relieved with the convoy intact, the siege broken, and the road held open behind the column.
forks.consequence: The factory town lives and the road stays open — and the March command contracts the unit to hold the route and the works it just saved, turning the relief into a standing garrison over a resupply line the besieger's survivors will spend the next season trying to cut again.

forks.name: OPERATION LATE COLUMN
forks.trigger: The garrison's clock expires before the relief arrives, or the column is bled below siege-breaking strength.
forks.consequence: The town falls or the relief arrives too weak to save it, and the works pass to the besieger. The follow-on is no longer a relief but a raid: hit the captured factory town and deny its output before the besieger can turn the very parts the relief was carrying against the March.

forks.name: OPERATION CUT BEHIND
forks.trigger: The relief reaches the town but the ambush belt closes the road behind it, trapping the column inside the wire.
forks.consequence: The siege is broken and the relief is now besieged with the garrison it saved — the road re-cut, the convoy spent, and two forces penned in a town that cannot be resupplied. The unit must now break out the way it broke in, against an enemy that let it through precisely to trap it.

storyElementSeed: At a halt between ambushes, a militia hauler driver counts the trucks still rolling against the manifest taped to his dash, then scratches out two numbers and writes a smaller one. He does not say it aloud. The engineer riding shotgun reads it over his shoulder and checks her own list against the parts the town asked for, doing the subtraction nobody wants to finish.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Get the convoy through and break the siege. The town needs what we're carrying more than it needs us, and a relief that arrives empty-handed is just a longer casualty list. Reach the wire in time and strong enough to lift the siege, or we've spent a battalion just delivering ourselves.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no aircraft to leapfrog the critical cargo. The light element runs the same road as everything else, only faster and thinner. It cannot skip the belt, so the split buys speed at the cost of a fast element small enough to be overwhelmed.

You have no hard currency to open the bridge. The approach to the local fighters must be made in promises and threats alone: slower, less convincing to draftees who have heard promises before, and more likely to fail at the killing ground.

title: OPERATION SHALLOW DRAFT
skeleton: an assault force landing without a usable DropPort must seize a working deep-water seaport intact across an amphibious approach, taking the port from the water and holding the quays against a counterattack before the heavy follow-on shipping can dock, where destroying the port to take it strands the whole campaign and the defender fights to wreck the cranes rather than hold the ground, so the crux is capturing the harbor whole and opening it to traffic under counterattack
inspiration: the amphibious seizure of a working deep-water port to land an army that cannot land without one — the assault on a defended harbor, mid-20th century
situation:
The {EMPLOYER} means to take {WORLD} back, and {WORLD}'s one good DropPort is a crater. The retreating Republic-remnant garrison cratered the spaceport's landing aprons in the campaign's first week. The {EMPLOYER}'s planners expected it, but they cannot wish it away: heavy DropShips cannot land on broken ground, and the world cannot be taken with only the few lances that a handful of intact pads will bear. {NPC:employer-contact}, the {EMPLOYER}'s landing-force commander, has another way in. The {DISTRICT} deep-water seaport, built before the Blackout and still working, is the only harbor on the coast that can dock the heavy sea transport the campaign's supplies actually run on. Take the port intact, open it to the {EMPLOYER}'s shipping, and the army lands over the quays. Take it wrecked, and the assault force that captured it starves on a coast it cannot reinforce.

The assault goes in from the water. The first wave, your unit and a {EMPLOYER} mechanized landing battalion, comes ashore from landing craft and shallow-draft boats onto the harbor approaches, because the port cannot be reached overland in time and the cratered DropPort cannot take the weight. {NPC:intel-source} reports the harbor held by a reinforced {TARGET_FACTION} garrison battalion with demolition charges set on the cranes, the moles, and the deep-water berths themselves. Note that this report is 5 to 12 days old. Every sign says the garrison's orders are not to hold the port but to deny it: if they cannot keep the harbor, they will wreck it, and a wrecked deep-water port is months of repair the campaign does not have.

The terrain problem is the harbor itself, the working waterfront the assault must take without breaking. The deep-water berths, the cranes, the moles, and the channel, all the things that make the port worth a campaign, are fragile, fixed in place, and wired to blow. Fight through the waterfront with heavy fire and you win the quays but lose the harbor. The approaches are shallow coastal water and tidal flat, where the landing craft run aground and the assault wades the last stretch under fire. Behind the port is the {DISTRICT} dock district, dense and built-up, where the garrison's reserve waits to counterattack the moment the first wave is committed at the water's edge.

The clock is the follow-on shipping. The {EMPLOYER}'s heavy transports are already inbound to the coast and cannot wait offshore. They must dock at a working, secured harbor within the window or turn back and leave the first wave ashore alone. The first wave must take the port, stop the demolitions, hold the quays through the counterattack, and open the channel to traffic, all before the ships carrying the rest of the army arrive to find a harbor either ready for them or burning.

objectives.primary: Seize the deep-water seaport intact and open it to the {EMPLOYER}'s follow-on shipping before the transport window closes. Keep the berths, cranes, and channel working, and the harbor secured.
objectives.secondary: Stop the garrison from blowing the port equipment. Keep the cranes, moles, deep-water berths, and channel whole, not won as rubble.
objectives.bonus: Hold the high ground in the dock district so the secured port has a defensible perimeter for the army landing behind the first wave.

complications.name: The Wired Harbor
complications.text: The cranes, moles, and deep-water berths are all wired with charges. The garrison means to deny the port if it cannot hold it, and one charge fired on the wrong berth can cost the campaign its only deep-water way in.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The key port equipment carries demolition charges the garrison can fire when it decides to deny the port. Heavy weapons fire near the waterfront can also set them off. Capturing the demolition control points before the garrison decides to blow the port is the only sure way to keep the harbor whole.

complications.name: Assault from the Water
complications.text: The first wave comes ashore from landing craft across shallow coastal water and tidal flat, running aground short and wading the last stretch under fire. There is no DropPort to land on and no other way in.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The assault lands light and exposed at the water's edge, with heavy support and resupply coming only over the beach until the port opens. The landing ground is fixed and exposed, and the tide controls where and when craft can ground. The first wave fights understrength until it can open the harbor to its own reinforcements.

complications.name: The Counterattack Clock
complications.text: The garrison's reserve waits in the dock district to strike the moment the first wave is committed to the waterfront. The follow-on shipping waits offshore and cannot loiter. The first wave must take, hold, and open the port in the gap between those two pressures.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A garrison counterattack launches once the assault commits to the harbor, hitting the first wave at its most exposed. A separate transport-window clock runs down to the shipping's arrival or turn-back. The port must be secured and opened within that window, and the counterattack is timed to stop exactly that.

decisionPoints.name: How to Take the Waterfront
decisionPoints.context: The harbor must be captured without being broken, by a first wave landing light from the water, against a garrison ready to wreck the quays. The method you choose decides whether the port opens whole or is won as a ruin the campaign cannot use.

options.title: Rush the Demolition Controls
advantages: Drive straight for the demolition control points, since taking the triggers before the garrison pulls them is the only sure way to keep the harbor whole
A port captured intact opens to the shipping on schedule and the campaign lands
Wrecks the garrison's whole denial plan in one stroke if it works
disadvantages: A headlong rush from the water's edge to the controls runs the first wave through the garrison's prepared waterfront defenses at speed
If the garrison reads the rush in time, it fires the charges before the controls are taken: the worst outcome, reached fast
The wave is at its most committed and most exposed when the counterattack comes
options.consequence: You bet everything on speed to the triggers. The harbor is saved whole or wrecked in the first hour, and the counterattack finds a wave strung out toward the controls either way.

costs.resource: the first wave's cohesion, spent rushing prepared defenses to reach the demolition controls before they are pulled
costs.risk: the garrison fires the charges as the wave closes, and the campaign loses its harbor to a demolition reached one minute too late

options.title: Clear It Methodically
advantages: Clear the waterfront carefully, disarming charges and clearing defenders berth by berth with minimal heavy fire near the cranes
Gives the best chance of taking the harbor genuinely intact
A cleared waterfront is a defensible one when the counterattack comes
disadvantages: Careful is slow, and the transport window does not wait: a port secured intact but late is a port the shipping has already turned away from
Slow clearing gives the garrison time to organize both its demolition and its counterattack
Every hour the first wave fights on the waterfront is an hour it is not opening the channel
options.consequence: You refuse to break the prize and pay in time. The harbor comes through whole if it comes through in time, and the transport window, not the garrison, may be the thing that beats a careful assault.

costs.resource: the transport window, drawn down by the extra hours careful clearing costs over a rush
costs.risk: the port is secured intact but too late, the shipping turns back, and the first wave holds a perfect empty harbor alone

options.title: Seize the Channel First
advantages: Take the harbor mouth and channel approaches first, the moles, the channel forts, the tugs, so the port can start opening even while the inner waterfront is still contested
Lets the follow-on shipping start its run the moment the channel is held, beating the window
Splits the garrison between the mouth and the quays
disadvantages: Securing the channel before the inner harbor leaves the cranes and berths in the garrison's hands the longest, so the charges stay live
A split assault is weaker at both the mouth and the waterfront
Shipping sent toward a channel whose berths are not yet secured is sailing toward a possible demolition
options.consequence: You open the door before you clear the house, racing the window by starting the harbor's opening early. The shipping comes on faster, toward a waterfront that may still be wired when it arrives.

costs.resource: the first wave's strength, split between seizing the channel and clearing the berths the charges still cover
costs.risk: the shipping commits to a channel whose berths blow as it arrives, and the campaign's transports sail into a wrecked harbor under fire

decisionPoints.name: The Garrison Counterattack
decisionPoints.context: The dock-district reserve strikes as the first wave commits to the waterfront: a battalion-scale counterattack aimed at throwing the assault back into the water before the port can open. The first wave is light, the shipping is inbound, and the charges may still be live behind the fighting.

options.title: Hold the Quays
advantages: Stand on the captured waterfront and break the counterattack on the ground that matters, the berths the shipping needs
Holding the quays keeps the port ready to open the instant the counterattack is beaten
Refuses to give back the one thing the whole assault was for
disadvantages: A light first wave holding fixed ground against a fresh battalion is a hard, bloody stand with the water at its back
Heavy defensive fire on the quays risks the very charges and cranes the wave is protecting
If the line breaks, it breaks with the assault pinned against a harbor it cannot retreat across
options.consequence: You plant yourself on the prize and dare the garrison to take it back. The quays hold and the port opens, or the wave is broken on the waterfront with the shipping arriving to watch, and the cranes caught in the middle either way.

costs.resource: the first wave's strength, spent holding fixed quays against a fresh battalion with the sea at its back
costs.risk: a fixed stand on the waterfront fought with heavy fire wrecks the cranes the wave is dying to protect

options.title: Counterattack into the District
advantages: Meet the counterattack with a mobile blow into the dock district, breaking up the garrison's reserve before it can mass on the quays
Fighting forward of the waterfront keeps the heavy combat away from the wired berths
A successful counterattack can shatter the garrison's last organized reserve and decide the harbor
disadvantages: A light first wave pushing into a dense built-up district may be swallowed by it, away from the port it must hold
Committing forward leaves the captured waterfront and its demolition controls thinly held
If the counterattack fails, the garrison takes the quays the wave left to attack it
options.consequence: You answer the counterattack by attacking it, keeping the fight off the cranes and betting mobility against a fresh battalion in its own streets. You win the harbor by breaking the reserve, or lose it by overreaching into the district.

costs.resource: the security of the captured waterfront, thinned to mount a counterattack into the dock district
costs.risk: the counterattack is swallowed by the built-up district and the garrison retakes the lightly held quays behind it

options.title: Open the Port Under Fire
advantages: Commit everything to opening the channel and the first berths while the counterattack is still building, getting the shipping docking before the garrison can close the door
A working berth landing the follow-on turns the whole battle: the army arrives in the middle of the counterattack
Wins the campaign clock outright if it works
disadvantages: Opening the port while a counterattack is underway means working the cranes and channel under direct fire
The first arriving transports are huge, slow, and helpless if a berth blows or the counterattack reaches the waterfront
Putting opening ahead of holding risks losing both if the counterattack breaks through
options.consequence: You race to land the army into the teeth of the counterattack, betting that reinforcement arriving mid-battle beats a clean defensive stand. The harbor opens under fire and the follow-on saves the wave, or a berth blows under a docking transport and the gamble takes the campaign down with it.

costs.resource: the first wave's ability to hold cleanly, all spent forcing the port open while the counterattack is still live
costs.risk: a transport docks into a berth that blows, or the counterattack reaches the waterfront mid-docking, and the campaign loses its harbor and its first reinforcement together

entries.event: Alarm: the first wave's landing craft cross the start line toward the harbor approaches. The garrison's coastal positions open fire on the shallow water as the boats run for the tidal flat.
The first wave runs aground short and wades ashore onto the harbor approaches under fire. The assault on the waterfront begins, and the garrison's demolition parties move to their firing points.
Lead elements reach the inner waterfront. The demolition control points and the cranes are in contact. The garrison's denial decision is now live, and charges may fire at any moment.
The garrison counterattacks from the dock district against the committed first wave: a battalion-scale blow aimed at the waterfront before the port can open.
The follow-on shipping reaches the coast and starts its run to the harbor mouth. It needs a held channel and a secured berth, or it holds offshore against its fuel and turns back.
The transport window closes. The follow-on shipping either docks at a secured, working harbor or turns back and leaves the first wave ashore alone.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The transport window decides the campaign. The follow-on shipping docks at a working, secured deep-water harbor within {TRANSPORT_WINDOW} hours or it turns back, and the first wave is left ashore without the army it landed to let in. But the window is only half the deadline. A harbor opened on time but wrecked is no harbor, and a harbor kept whole but opened late is no help. The first wave must take the port intact, stop the demolitions, hold the quays through the counterattack, and open the channel to traffic before the ships arrive, or the assault that captured {WORLD}'s only deep-water way in has captured a coast it cannot hold.

opforSketch.composition: A reinforced {TARGET_FACTION} garrison battalion holding the harbor: a BattleMech company (Regular, dug into the dock district and the waterfront), an armor company with coastal-defense positions and the dock-district counterattack reserve (this is the combined-arms weight — coastal armor on the approaches and a mobile armored reserve for the counterstroke), combat engineers manning the port demolitions, and infantry throughout the built-up waterfront. The garrison's defining asset is the wired harbor, not its numbers. Behavioral breakpoint: the garrison fights to deny rather than to hold — it will fire the demolitions and trade the port for rubble if it cannot keep the harbor, and its counterattack is timed to force exactly that choice on the assault.
opforSketch.behavior: The garrison defends a harbor it is prepared to destroy. It holds the waterfront to buy time for the demolition decision, counterattacks from the dock district to throw the first wave back before the port can open, and treats the cranes and berths as a denial asset, not ground to be held at all costs. Its victory condition is a wrecked harbor or a thrown-back assault; the assault's whole problem is that the defender would rather break the prize than lose it. The garrison's engineers are the real enemy, and the demolition control points are the real objective.

forks.name: OPERATION DEEP BERTH
forks.trigger: The port seized intact, opened to the follow-on shipping in the window, and the dock district held.
forks.consequence: The army lands over the secured quays and the campaign for {WORLD} truly begins — with the unit holding the harbor it took, the lifeline for everything that follows, against a garrison remnant that knows the port's wiring and will try to take back by raid what it could not deny by demolition.

forks.name: OPERATION BROKEN MOLE
forks.trigger: The harbor is wrecked, the window closes with the port unsecured, or the counterattack throws the first wave back.
forks.consequence: The follow-on shipping turns back and the first wave is stranded ashore on a hostile coast with no deep-water entry behind it. The mission collapses into a fighting evacuation off the beach, lifting what it can of a landing force the campaign can no longer reinforce, with the army that was meant to land turning for home.

forks.name: OPERATION SALT BERTH
forks.trigger: The port is taken but partly demolished, or the first transport is lost docking under fire.
forks.consequence: The {EMPLOYER} lands its army over a half-wrecked harbor working at a fraction of capacity — every ton through a damaged channel and a single surviving berth, under repair and under threat. The unit must hold and rebuild a crippled port while the campaign it serves runs on a logistics line one demolition charge wide.

storyElementSeed: A {EMPLOYER} sapper, soaked to the chest from the wade ashore, kneels at the base of a harbor crane and traces the demolition wiring with two fingers, following it back toward the firing point — and finds, taped to the charge, a handwritten note in the garrison engineer's hand listing the firing order, left either out of professional habit or as a last courtesy from one engineer to whoever came after. He reads it, and starts cutting in reverse.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Take the harbor whole and open it to the convoy. The Commonwealth's army lands over those quays or it does not land at all, and a deep-water port is not something you win in pieces. Secure the berths, stop the charges, and have the channel open when the ships arrive, or we have stormed a beach to nowhere.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no shipping of your own to coordinate an early approach. The follow-on transports run on the {EMPLOYER}'s schedule and cannot be waved in early on a held channel. Securing the mouth first buys position but not time, and the window stays where it was.

You have no port-operations crew landed with the first wave. Opening the harbor falls to the assault troops working the cranes themselves under fire. Add a delay to bring any berth online, and accept that fighting men make slow dock workers.

title: OPERATION LONG WATCH
skeleton: a Clan garrison holding a frontier world by zellbrigen must defend it against a rival Clan's escalating series of formal Trials of Possession, where each won Trial costs the defender warriors and machines it cannot replace from a frontier with no reinforcement while a loss forfeits the world piece by piece, so the crux is husbanding an unreplaceable force across a sequence of honor-bound single combats rather than one decisive battle
inspiration: the frontier garrison worn down by a sequence of formal challenges it cannot decline and cannot resupply — the wasting defense of a distant march, antiquity
situation:
The world the Cluster won is the world the Cluster must keep. {WORLD} sits at the raw edge of the Wolf Empire's frontier, taken two years ago and garrisoned ever since by your command: a reinforced Cluster, bid down at the conquest and never brought back to strength, because the frontier swallows reinforcements and the Empire's supply lines are long. {NPC:employer-contact}, your Star Colonel, holds the world for the Khan. You hold the {DISTRICT} highland keep and the industrial works it guards, the seat of the garrison and the prize of the world. And now the Jade Falcons have come to take it the proper way.

The Falcons do not raid. {NPC:opfor-commander}, their commanding officer, has opened a campaign of Trials: a run of formal Trials of Possession, cried one after another, each for a piece of {WORLD}. A Trial for an outlying holdfast, a Trial for a mining district, a Trial for the keep itself, each one bigger than the last, all fought under the rules of zellbrigen. {NPC:intel-source} reads the Falcon plan clearly. They mean to take {WORLD} not in one battle but in a slow, wearing series, betting that a frontier garrison with no reinforcement cannot afford the warriors and machines that even winning Trials costs. Every Trial the garrison wins, it wins at a price it cannot repay. Every Trial it loses, it gives up a piece of the world. The Falcons can replace what they spend. The garrison cannot.

The terrain problem is the highland approaches to the keep, the ground the Trials are fought on. The {DISTRICT} keep sits atop a mountain massif, ringed by high passes and ridges that funnel any challenge into a handful of defensible grounds. The terrain favors a defender who gets to choose the ground of each Trial, and under the Forms that choice is itself a weapon: pick well, and you can make a Trial cost the challenger more than the prize is worth. But the keep's own works, the industry that makes {WORLD} worth holding, sit exposed at the heart of the massif, and a Trial fought carelessly across them damages the very thing the garrison is defending.

The garrison's strength is limited and falling: the Cluster's surviving Stars, the machines the techs can keep running with no parts coming from anywhere, and the warriors who must answer each Trial in person. There is no relief on the frontier. The Falcons know it. The campaign is not a battle to be won but a slow drain to be outlasted, and the Falcons are counting the garrison's machines as carefully as the garrison is.

objectives.primary: Hold {WORLD} and its keep against the Falcon campaign of Trials. Keep the world for the Khan and the keep and its works unforfeited, until the Falcons run out of will to keep challenging.
objectives.secondary: Conserve the garrison's irreplaceable force. Win the Trials that must be won at the lowest possible cost in warriors and machines, and refuse or shift the ground of the ones that need not be fought head-on.
objectives.bonus: Break the Falcon commander's campaign at its root. Win a decisive Trial against {NPC:opfor-commander} directly, or make a victory so costly that it ends the Falcon appetite for {WORLD} for a generation.

complications.name: The Shrinking Force
complications.text: Every Trial costs the garrison machines and warriors it cannot replace. The frontier sends no reinforcements, and the techs work miracles on a shrinking stock of parts. A won Trial is a victory the garrison pays for in strength it will never get back.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The garrison's available force is a fixed pool that never refills, tracked across the Trials. Every Trial, won or lost, draws from it. Damaged machines can be repaired only as far as the parts allow, and that margin shrinks with each fight. The campaign is graded on the force left standing at the end, not on Trials won.

complications.name: The Forms Bind Both Sides
complications.text: Zellbrigen governs the Trials: bids, single combats, and the defender's right to choose the ground. The Forms are both a limit and a weapon. Honored, they cost the garrison. Used well, they can make a Trial too expensive for the challenger.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Trials are fought under zellbrigen by default. The defender chooses the ground of each Trial, which shapes its cost. Breaking the Forms is possible but carries an honor cost that affects the garrison's standing, the Falcon response, and how the campaign ends. Bidding well, committing only what a Trial needs, conserves the force.

complications.name: The Prize Is Exposed
complications.text: The keep's industrial works, the reason {WORLD} is worth a campaign, sit at the heart of the ground the Trials are fought over. A Trial fought carelessly across them damages the world the garrison is bleeding to keep.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Trials fought on or near the works risk damaging the world's secondary value. Choosing ground away from the works protects the prize but may give up tactical advantage. Defending the works directly protects them at the cost of fighting on ground the Falcons may prefer.

decisionPoints.name: How to Answer the Trials
decisionPoints.context: The Falcons cry Trial after Trial, each for a piece of {WORLD}, each one bigger than the last. The garrison cannot win them all at a price it can pay, and cannot refuse them all without giving up the world. The standing answer you set now decides how the shrinking force is spent.

options.title: Answer Each in Full
advantages: Meet every Trial with the strength to win it cleanly under the Forms, keeping honor spotless and giving up no piece of {WORLD}
A garrison that wins every Trial decisively may break the Falcon will before its own force runs out
The proudest defense, and the one that keeps the world whole if the force holds out
disadvantages: Winning every Trial in full spends the force fastest, bleeding machines the garrison cannot replace at every challenge
The Falcons can replace what they lose, so a Trial-for-Trial attrition race is one the frontier garrison is built to lose
A force spent winning the early Trials has nothing left for the decisive one
options.consequence: You answer honor with honor and meet the campaign head-on. You keep {WORLD} whole for as long as the force lasts, and the Falcons are betting, with reason, that their stock outlasts the garrison's pride.

costs.resource: the garrison's force, spent at full rate to win every Trial cleanly: machines and warriors the frontier will never replace
costs.risk: an attrition race against a Clan that can reinforce, fought until the garrison's hands are empty while the Falcons still have stock

options.title: Bid Low and Conserve
advantages: Answer each Trial with the bare minimum the Forms require: bid low, choose ground that favors the defender, and spend as little as a win allows
Stretches the force across far more Trials than answering in full would allow
The choice of ground turns the terrain into the extra strength the garrison's numbers cannot provide
disadvantages: Bidding low risks losing a Trial outright, and a lost Trial gives up a piece of {WORLD}
Conserving means giving up the early holdfasts and districts to keep strength for the keep, trading the world's edges for its heart
A garrison seen bidding lower and lower may tempt the Falcons to escalate faster, smelling weakness
options.consequence: You fight to outlast rather than to win, spending the force a little at a time instead of by the handful and giving up ground to keep strength. You keep the keep by letting the edges go, shrinking the defense toward the prize and betting the Falcons tire before they reach the core.

costs.resource: the outlying districts and holdfasts of {WORLD}, given up Trial by Trial to conserve the force for the keep
costs.risk: bidding too low loses a Trial that mattered, and the conserving gives up the very ground that made the world worth holding

options.title: Force a Decisive Trial
advantages: Refuse the war of attrition: challenge {NPC:opfor-commander} to a single great Trial for all of {WORLD}, staking the world on one combat instead of a long, wearing series
If the Falcons accept and lose, the campaign ends in one stroke and the garrison is spared the long bleed
The boldest answer, and the one that best fits the Falcon love of a decisive test
disadvantages: Staking the whole world on one Trial risks losing {WORLD} in an afternoon to a single defeat
The Falcons need not accept, and a refused grand challenge may be read as the garrison's desperation
Committing the garrison's best to one combat leaves nothing if it fails and the Falcons press the ruin
options.consequence: You try to collapse the long campaign into a single honorable test, betting everything on one combat rather than the slow drain. You win the world clean or lose it whole, and the Falcons decide whether to grant the gamble.

costs.resource: the whole world, staked on a single Trial, with no force left to spend if the decisive combat is lost
costs.risk: a refused or lost grand Trial throws away in one combat what the slow defense might have held for a year

decisionPoints.name: The Trial for the Keep
decisionPoints.context: The Falcons cry their biggest Trial yet, for the keep itself, the seat of the garrison and the works that are the world's prize. The ground is the garrison's to choose, the force its to bid, and its strength is whatever the earlier Trials have left. This is the one that cannot be given up.

options.title: Fight on the High Passes
advantages: Choose the high passes ringing the keep, terrain that funnels the Falcon challenge into defensible single-combat ground and keeps the fighting off the works
The passes favor the defender and protect the prize from damage
A Trial won here is won away from the works the garrison is bleeding to keep
disadvantages: Fighting forward at the passes commits the garrison's strength away from the keep itself
The passes are exposed ground for a garrison whose numbers are already thin
A loss at the passes leaves the keep behind a beaten line
options.consequence: You fight for the keep on the ground that protects it, spending your honor-bound combats in the high passes where the terrain stands in for the numbers you lack. The keep and its works come through whole if the passes hold.

costs.resource: the garrison's strength, committed forward to the passes and away from the keep it defends
costs.risk: a defeat at the passes leaves the keep undefended behind a beaten line, with too little force left to form another

options.title: Defend the Works Directly
advantages: Hold the Trial on the keep's own ground, where the garrison fights from prepared positions it knows and the Falcons must come to it
Concentrates the thin force at the one point that cannot be lost
No risk of being drawn forward and cut off from the prize
disadvantages: A Trial fought across the works risks damaging the industry that is the whole point of holding {WORLD}
Giving up the choice of approach lets the Falcons fight on ground nearer the prize than the garrison would like
Winning the keep while wrecking its works is a hollow victory the Khan will note
options.consequence: You make your stand on the prize itself, accepting the risk to the works for the certainty of fighting where you cannot be outflanked. The keep is held, and whole, if the garrison's fire discipline holds with it.

costs.resource: the works' intact value, risked by fighting the decisive Trial across the works themselves
costs.risk: the Trial damages the industry, and the garrison wins a keep whose prize it broke in the winning

options.title: Stake It on a Champion
advantages: Narrow the Trial to single combat between the garrison's best warrior and the Falcon's: the purest form of the Forms, and the cheapest in force if it is won
One combat decides the keep, sparing the rest of the thin garrison
A champion's win against the Falcon's best can break the whole campaign's momentum
disadvantages: Staking the keep on one warrior risks losing it to a single defeat or one unlucky stroke
The garrison's best, lost in the combat, is the worst possible loss for a force that cannot replace warriors
The Falcons may field a champion bred and trained for exactly this, against a garrison's tired best
options.consequence: You narrow the defense of the keep to one warrior and one combat, spending the least force for the highest stake. The keep stands on a single champion's skill, and so does everything the garrison has bled two years to hold.

costs.resource: the garrison's finest warrior and machine, staked on a single combat for the keep
costs.risk: the champion falls, and the keep, the world, and the garrison's irreplaceable best are lost in one stroke

entries.event: Alarm: the Falcons cry the campaign's first Trial, a challenge for an outlying holdfast, with the Forms invoked and the bid laid down. The garrison's answer to this first Trial sets the pattern the Falcons will read.

The first Trial is resolved, and the garrison's force takes its first cut. The Falcon commander weighs the garrison's cost and cries the next Trial to match: bigger if the garrison answered in full, harder if it bid low and lost.

Trial for a mining district. The Falcons test whether the garrison will give up the edges to conserve the keep. The choice of ground and the bid here reveal the garrison's strategy to a watching enemy.

The garrison's force is visibly drawn down. The techs report which damaged machines can and cannot be put back on the line. The garrison's true remaining strength becomes the central fact of the campaign.
The Falcons cry the Trial for the keep, the decisive challenge of the campaign, for the seat of the garrison and the world's prize. The ground, the bid, and the form of the answer can no longer wait.

Falcon turning point: the Trial for the keep is resolved, the campaign decided by what force the garrison had left to spend on it. Past here, the Falcons either withdraw beaten or hold the world they wore down.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: There is no clock, only the force. The campaign ends when one side's will or strength to keep fighting Trials runs out, and the Falcons can replace what they spend while the garrison cannot. The hard limit is the garrison's exhaustion: the point where the shrinking force can no longer answer a cried Trial with enough strength to win it. Past that point, every further Trial gives up a piece of {WORLD} the garrison cannot defend, and the world is lost not in a battle but in a slow drain, worn down challenge by challenge until there is nothing left to bid. Holding {WORLD} means making the Falcons tire of paying before the garrison runs out of warriors to pay with.

opforSketch.composition: A Jade Falcon assault force conducting a campaign of Trials: a reinforced Cluster's worth of front-line Clan BattleMechs (Veteran-to-Elite, OmniMechs and second-line designs), committed Trial by Trial under zellbrigen rather than all at once. This is a MECH_ONLY campaign by the Forms — Trial of Possession, warrior against warrior, no combined arms by the conventions both sides observe. The Falcon strength is depth: they can replace what they lose where the garrison cannot. Behavioral breakpoint: the Falcons honor zellbrigen rigorously and escalate their Trials as they read the garrison's cost, pressing hardest where the garrison bids low; their will to continue breaks only if a Trial costs them more than {WORLD} is worth to their honor.
opforSketch.behavior: The Falcons wage an honor war of attrition. They cry escalating Trials, honor the Forms, and bet that a frontier garrison cannot afford even its victories. They read the garrison's every bid and choice of ground, escalating to exploit weakness and husbanding their own depth knowing they have more of it. They do not seek a single decisive battle unless the garrison forces one; their strategy is the wasting ledger, and their weakness is that a Trial made costly enough — or a champion thrown down and beaten — can wound the Falcon honor that drives the whole campaign and end their appetite for the world.

forks.name: OPERATION UNBROKEN KEEP
forks.trigger: The Falcon campaign broken or exhausted with the keep held and the garrison's core force intact.
forks.consequence: {WORLD} stays the Khan's, and the garrison that held it against a Clan campaign of Trials is now a proven frontier command — tasked to hold the world through whatever the Falcons send next, and watched by the Empire's own rivals who marked how thin the victory ran.

forks.name: OPERATION WORN AWAY
forks.trigger: The wasting ledger empties and the keep is forfeited, or the decisive Trial is lost.
forks.consequence: The Falcons take {WORLD} the way they planned to, worn down piece by piece, and the garrison's survivors are the remnant of a Cluster that held a frontier two years and lost it to a ledger. The follow-on is a fighting withdrawal off the world, salvaging what warriors and machines the long defense left, back toward an Empire whose frontier just contracted by one world.

forks.name: OPERATION BROKEN FORMS
forks.trigger: The Forms break down — a Trial dishonored by either side, or the campaign degenerates into open battle.
forks.consequence: Zellbrigen collapses and the wasting Trial becomes a real war the thin garrison is even less equipped to fight — no more single combats, no more chosen ground, just a Falcon force with the depth to overwhelm a garrison that can no longer hide its weakness behind the Forms. The unit fights for the keep with honor spent and numbers against it.

storyElementSeed: In the keep's repair bay, a tech chalks the running-machine count on the wall the way she has every morning since the Trials began. The number is lower than yesterday. She does not erase the old numbers; the column of them climbs the wall behind her like a record of subtraction, and the warriors walking past to answer the next Trial read it without slowing and without comment.

clan.objectives.primary: Hold this world for the Khan against the Falcon's Trials. They mean to wear us down to nothing one challenge at a time, counting our machines as we count them. We cannot replace what we spend; they can. So we spend it dearly, we choose our ground, and we make the Falcons weary of the price before we run out of warriors to charge it. The world stays ours, or we leave it with our honor and nothing else.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no fortified ground of your own choosing to stake the grand Trial on. The decisive combat must be fought wherever the Falcons will accept it, giving up the defender's choice of ground, the one advantage a thin garrison cannot spare.

You have no parts reserve to repair the works after the fighting. Damage done to the works in the Trial cannot be undone. The garrison wins a keep whose prize stays broken, and the Khan inherits a world worth less than the one bid for.

title: OPERATION HARD FRONTIER
skeleton: a security force too small for the frontier must defend a string of dispersed settlements along a raw border against raids that strike the gaps in its coverage, where concentrating to hold any one point opens the others and the raiders read the force's dispositions to hit wherever it is not, so the crux is allocating an insufficient mobile reserve across an indefensible frontage rather than holding a fixed line
inspiration: the cavalry frontier — too few troops covering too many settlements against fast raiders who strike the undefended gap, the dispersed-post border defense of arid frontiers, 19th century
situation:
The {DISTRICT} frontier is a line on a map and nothing on the ground. When the Republic's authority lifted from this stretch of {WORLD} in the Blackout, it left a string of {SETTLEMENT_COUNT} settlements, farming holdings, water bores, and a few mining camps, spread across 400 kilometers of dry border country with no garrison and no warning system. Your employer is {EMPLOYER}, the frontier settlements' protective league, and your contact is {NPC:employer-contact}. They have scraped together the fee for a security contract, and your unit is what the fee buys: one reinforced company, mostly mobile, to defend a frontage a whole regiment could not hold as a line. The settlements expect protection. The math says protection, in the way they mean it, does not exist.

The raiders understand this better than the league does. {NPC:intel-source} reports a fast raider band, Blackout opportunists working the border from the open country beyond it: a mixed force of light 'Mechs, hover armor, and technicals built for speed and reach. Note that this report is 4 to 12 days old. They do not mass up and they do not hold ground. They strike a settlement, take what they came for, and are gone across the border before any concentrated force can arrive. And they read the security force's movements: every patrol pattern, every reaction posture, every place the company gathers tells them where the gap is, and the gap is where they hit. The band is not trying to beat the company. It is trying to be wherever the company is not.

The terrain problem is the frontier's sheer openness: distance and spread. The desert border gives the raiders speed and gives the defender nothing to hold. The settlements are scattered across hundreds of kilometers of hardpan, scrub, and broken gully country. The border itself is unmarked and impossible to fence. The open ground favors the fast raider who picks the time and place over the defender tied to fixed points. There is no line to man, no chokepoint to hold, no terrain that funnels the raids, only distance, and a mobile reserve too small to be everywhere that distance demands.

The company cannot defend all {SETTLEMENT_COUNT} settlements at once and cannot predict which one the raiders will hit. Concentrate to protect the most valuable, and the rest are open. Spread out to cover them all, and the company is too thin everywhere to stop anything. The contract is a problem of allocation: where to put a force too small for the job, on a frontier that cannot be held as a line, against an enemy whose whole method is to strike where the force is not.

objectives.primary: Keep the frontier livable through the contract. Hold settlement losses below the level that breaks the league, and make raiding cost the raiders more than it earns them.
objectives.secondary: Build a warning-and-response system that lets a small mobile reserve cover a large frontage: outposts, patrols, and local levies that turn distance from the raiders' ally into the defender's.
objectives.bonus: Find and break the raider band's base across the border, or cut the local network feeding it intelligence, so the frontier is secured at its source instead of just patrolled.

complications.name: A Frontier Too Big to Hold
complications.text: One company, {SETTLEMENT_COUNT} settlements, 400 kilometers of open border. The force cannot hold a line because there is no line, and cannot cover every point because there are too many. Every place it concentrates leaves a gap somewhere else.
complications.mechanicalEffect: At any moment the company can only reach a fraction of the frontage. Settlements outside current coverage are exposed. Concentrating the reserve protects its area and widens the gaps elsewhere. Spreading it out thins the response below what it takes to stop a raid. Allocation is the central, repeating decision.

complications.name: The Raiders Read the Gaps
complications.text: The band watches the security force's patterns and strikes wherever it is not. Predictable movements are an invitation. The raiders' intelligence on the company is as good as the company's on them, and maybe better.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Raid events hit the settlement with the least coverage and the slowest response time, weighted by how predictable the company's movements are. Varying patterns and running feints can mislead the raiders. Falling into routine lets them strike freely. The band reacts to the defender's posture rather than fighting it head-on.

complications.name: Distance Is the Enemy's Ally
complications.text: The open frontier gives the fast raiders speed and reach and gives the defender only ground to cross. A raid is over before a concentrated force can arrive. The band fights only to break away, then vanishes across a border no one can fence.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The raiders are faster than the company's average reaction speed, so raids finish and break contact before the reserve arrives unless it is already positioned within reach. Chasing them across the border is possible but stretches the force and may go beyond the contract. Distance is beaten by the warning system and pre-positioning, not by speed alone.

decisionPoints.name: How to Cover the Frontier
decisionPoints.context: A force too small, a frontier too big to hold, and an enemy that hits the gaps. The company's standing setup, chosen now and read by the raiders, decides which settlements are protected, which are exposed, and whether distance helps the defender or the raider.

options.title: Concentrate the Reserve
advantages: Hold the company as a single mobile fist at the frontier's center, ready to strike hard at any raid within reach
A concentrated reserve can wipe out a raiding band if it can reach one in time
Protects the most valuable settlements and gives the raiders a real risk to face where the fist can fall
disadvantages: A central reserve cannot reach the frontier's edges before a raid is over, so the distant settlements are simply uncovered
The raiders read the concentration and strike the far gaps where the fist will never arrive
Concentration protects a fraction of the frontage and writes off the rest
options.consequence: You defend what you can reach and dare the raiders to come within range of the fist. The central settlements are safe and the edges are open, and the band hits the edges because the company showed it where they were.

costs.resource: the frontier's edges: settlements beyond the central reserve's reach, left uncovered by the concentration
costs.risk: the raiders simply strike the far gaps the fist cannot reach, and the company protects a third of the frontier while the rest burns

options.title: Spread Out to Cover
advantages: Break the company into settlement detachments and patrols so every settlement has some protection and some warning
No settlement is wholly uncovered, and the raiders face resistance wherever they strike
A presence across the frontage reassures the league and complicates the raiders' planning
disadvantages: A spread-out company is weak everywhere, with each detachment too small to stop a determined raid, only to report it
The raiders can mass against any one thinned detachment and overwhelm it
Spreading out trades the ability to win a fight for the ability to witness one
options.consequence: You spread out to be present everywhere and decisive nowhere. Every settlement has a guard and none has enough, and the raiders learn they can beat any one detachment by bringing more than it has.

costs.resource: the company's massed strength: broken into detachments too small to stop a raid, only to slow it and report it
costs.risk: the raiders mass on one thinned post and destroy it, turning the defender's presence into the defender's casualties

options.title: Build the Warning System
advantages: Spend the early contract not on patrolling but on a warning-and-response system: outposts, signal relays, armed local levies, and a small fast reserve held ready to act on the warning
Turns distance from the raiders' ally into the defender's, because a raid spotted early is a raid the reserve can reach
The lasting answer: a frontier that watches itself and a reserve that strikes on warning instead of guessing
disadvantages: Building the system takes time, and the settlements are being raided through it, so the early weeks are uncovered while the watchers are still being placed
The system leans on local levies, whose reliability and the raiders' informants both work against it
A reserve held ready to act on warning is a reserve not patrolling now, and the league wants to see protection today
options.consequence: You invest in seeing the frontier instead of holding it, betting that warning plus a fast reserve beats a presence everywhere. The system takes weeks to build and the raids do not pause for it, but a frontier that watches itself is the only kind one company can hold.

costs.resource: the early weeks of the contract, spent building the system while the settlements are raided through the gaps it does not yet cover
costs.risk: the levies are unreliable or penetrated by the raiders' informants, and the company has spent its time building a warning system that warns the enemy

decisionPoints.name: The Double Raid
decisionPoints.context: The band strikes two settlements at once, far apart. It is either a feint and a real blow, or two real blows, and the company cannot tell which in time. The reserve can reach one. Choose wrong and you lose a settlement you could have saved. Split to reach both and you reach neither in strength.

options.title: Commit to the Larger
advantages: Send the whole reserve to the more valuable settlement under attack and save it decisively
A concentrated response wipes out the raiding element there and warns the band off that area
Protects what matters most and takes the lesser loss cleanly
