disadvantages: The other settlement is written off, and if it was the real blow and the larger was the feint, the company sent its strength to the wrong place
The raiders learn the company will always cover the high-value target, and feint it every time
A settlement abandoned to save another is a league member who learns the contract plays favorites
options.consequence: You save the settlement you judge most worth saving and lose the other. It is the disciplined choice and a public one, and if the band feinted the prize to strike the gap, that discipline was exactly the predictability the raiders read.

costs.resource: the smaller settlement, written off to concentrate on the larger
costs.risk: the larger raid was the feint, and the company sent its whole reserve to the wrong place, losing the settlement it could have saved

options.title: Split the Reserve
advantages: Divide the reserve to respond to both raids at once, so neither settlement is abandoned
Denies the raiders the clean choice between feint and blow
A presence at both may scatter both raiding elements before they finish
disadvantages: A split reserve is two half-reserves, each possibly too weak to beat the raid it faces
If either raid is the band's main strength, the half-reserve sent against it may be overwhelmed
Splitting to cover everything is the spread-out trap in miniature, at the worst possible moment
options.consequence: You refuse to abandon either settlement and risk being too weak at both. Both raids are contested and neither is surely beaten, and the band finds out whether half the company is enough to stop it.

costs.resource: the reserve's massed strength, split between two raids and possibly too thin for either
costs.risk: a half-reserve meets the band's full strength and is overwhelmed, losing the settlement and a piece of the company with it

options.title: Race for the Border Instead
advantages: Let both raids run and drive the reserve hard for the border crossing the raiders must use to escape, catching the loaded, withdrawing band in the open where it is most vulnerable
Hitting the raiders on the way out can cost them more than defending either settlement
A band caught and mauled crossing back learns the frontier has teeth
disadvantages: Racing for the border abandons both settlements to the raids in progress, so the goods are taken and the damage done
The reserve must guess the crossing point right or catch nothing across a border no one can fence
Chasing them past the border may go beyond the contract and strand the company in the open country the raiders own
options.consequence: You give up saving the settlements to punish the raiders, betting that a band bled on the way home raids less next time. Both settlements take their losses and the raiders take theirs at the crossing, if the company guessed the border right.

costs.resource: both settlements under attack, abandoned to the raids to set an ambush on the band's escape route
costs.risk: the raiders cross where the reserve is not, and the company abandoned two settlements to catch nothing in the empty border country

entries.event: Alarm: a raid hits a settlement at the frontier's edge, fast, in and gone, the band striking a gap in the company's current coverage. By the time the report reaches the reserve, the raiders are already pulling out.

The settlement reports the take and the raiders' direction. The reserve, wherever it is, works out whether it can reach the next likely target or the border crossing in time. Usually it cannot reach the raid itself.
A second raid, far from the first, as the band exploits the company's reaction to the opening strike. The double-raid decision is now live and the reserve cannot cover both.
The raiders' pattern over the opening days becomes readable, and so does the company's. Whichever side has read the other better gets to choose the next ground.
The band's route back toward the border firms up. A pre-positioned reserve or a fast race may catch the loaded raiders in the open, the one place they are vulnerable.
Contract assessment: settlement losses counted against the league's breaking point, and the raiders' profit weighed against their cost. The frontier held or it did not, judged on who was where when.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: There is no single hour, only the league's patience and the raiders' math. The hard limit is the loss threshold: if settlement losses across the contract pass what the protective league can bear, the league breaks, the settlements scatter or make their own terms with the raiders, and the contract fails no matter how many single fights were won. The company's job is to keep the frontier livable, to make raiding cost more than it pays and keep losses below the breaking point, across a frontage it cannot hold as a line, against an enemy that strikes wherever the company is not. The frontier is kept by allocation and warning, or it is not kept at all.

opforSketch.composition: A fast Blackout raider band working the border: light and medium BattleMechs built for speed (Regular, hit-and-run doctrine), hover armor and fast technicals as the bulk of the striking force (this is the combined-arms weight — hover and wheeled raiders that out-range the defender across open ground), and mounted raider infantry for the settlement work. No DropShip presence in the contract area — the band bases across the border in open country. Its strength is mobility, reach, and intelligence on the defender. Behavioral breakpoint: the raiders never accept a stand-up fight with the concentrated reserve; they strike gaps, take their profit, and break for the border, fighting only to disengage and abandoning a raid the instant the reserve gets within reach.
opforSketch.behavior: The band raids the gaps and never the strength. It reads the company's dispositions and strikes wherever the reserve is not, feints to draw the reserve out of position, and times its raids to the defender's predictability. It fights only to escape, never to hold ground, and crosses an unfenceable border before a concentrated force can arrive. Its weaknesses are two: it is vulnerable when laden and withdrawing, caught in the open near the crossing, and it depends on local informants and a base across the border that, found and broken, would end the raiding at its source rather than its symptoms.

forks.name: OPERATION HELD LINE
forks.trigger: The frontier held through the contract with losses below threshold and the raiders' base or network broken.
forks.consequence: The league, its frontier intact, extends the unit to a standing garrison contract — and the broken raider band's survivors and rivals both test the new defense, while the warning net the company built becomes the model the league wants extended along the rest of its border.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN BORDER
forks.trigger: Settlement losses pass the league's breaking threshold and the protective league collapses.
forks.consequence: The frontier breaks: settlements scatter, sue the raiders for terms, or are abandoned, and the league that hired the company dissolves with its fee half-paid. The follow-on is an evacuation — lifting the holdouts who will not deal with the raiders off a frontier the contract could not hold.

forks.name: OPERATION INSIDE MEN
forks.trigger: The raiders' local informant network is found to reach inside the company's own warning net, or a levy detachment is turned.
forks.consequence: The net the company built to watch the frontier is watching it for the raiders too — the warning system penetrated, a levy post feeding the band the reserve's every move. The unit must root out the informants inside its own defense before it can trust a single report, while the raiders strike with perfect knowledge of where the company is not.

storyElementSeed: A reserve lance commander pins the frontier map to the inside of her cockpit and marks the night's raid with a grease pencil — the fourth mark this week, all of them in the gaps between her patrols, none of them where she was. She studies the pattern of her own absences taking shape on the map and understands, with a cold professionalism, that she is looking at the raiders' actual target list: the places she keeps choosing not to be.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no funds to equip and pay the warning system. The outposts and levies must be raised on the league's goodwill and the settlements' own people: slower to stand up, thinner where it counts, and more vulnerable to a raider band that can simply outbid the league for an informant.

You have no forward staging post near the border. The reserve must race from its central position, adding the distance that lets the loaded raiders cross before the intercept can close, so the ambush at the crossing becomes a stern chase that usually arrives empty.

title: OPERATION SECOND CITY
skeleton: an assault force must clear a defended industrial city block by block to break a dug-in garrison that has turned the urban core into a fortress and means to make the taking so ruinous and slow that the wider campaign stalls, where reducing the city by fire wins the streets and forfeits the industrial prize the campaign exists to seize, so the crux is methodical urban clearance that takes the works intact against a defender fighting to make the city cost more than it is worth
inspiration: the grinding battle for a fortified industrial city — block-by-block urban assault where the defender fights to make the city itself the trap, mid-20th century
situation:
The re-formed {EMPLOYER}'s campaign to reclaim {WORLD} has gone well everywhere except where it matters. The countryside fell in three weeks. The {DISTRICT} industrial city, {WORLD}'s second city and its manufacturing heart, the prize that makes the whole world worth a campaign, has not fallen at all. {NPC:employer-contact}, the {EMPLOYER}'s ground commander, holds every approach to it and cannot take it, because the {TARGET_FACTION} garrison holding the city has decided to make the {EMPLOYER} pay for it street by street. Your unit is committed to the assault that has to break the deadlock: into the city, into the close fight, to clear the urban core and take the works.

The garrison is dug in and in no hurry. {NPC:intel-source} reports a reinforced garrison battalion: Republic-remnant regulars stiffened by local volunteers, fighting from prepared positions throughout the city. Strongpoints in the factory complexes, anti-'Mech ambushes in the street canyons, and the whole industrial sprawl turned into a fortress of positions that cover each other. Note that this report is 6 to 14 days old. Every sign says the commander's aim is not to win but to make the {EMPLOYER} bleed: a defense built so that taking the city costs so much, and takes so long, that the {EMPLOYER}'s wider campaign, its budget, its timetable, its political will, runs out and stalls in the rubble of one city. The garrison is trading the city for the campaign.

The terrain problem is the industrial core, the prize the assault must take without destroying. The {DISTRICT} works are dense urban-industrial ground: factory halls, foundries, refineries, and the worker districts around them, with streets 10 to 20 meters wide, multi-story ferrocrete throughout, short sightlines, and ambush range point-blank. The works are what the campaign wants: the foundries running, the tooling intact, the skilled workers in place. An assault that clears the city by leveling it wins the streets and throws away the reason for the war. The {EMPLOYER} cannot simply flatten the industrial heart it crossed the stars to seize. The defenders know it, and they fight from inside the very works the {EMPLOYER} dares not destroy.

The clock is the campaign itself. The {EMPLOYER}'s reclamation runs on a Parliament-voted budget and a timetable the provincial rivals are watching. Every week the second city holds is a week the campaign burns money and credibility it cannot spare. The garrison is counting those weeks as carefully as the {EMPLOYER}'s paymasters are. The assault must clear the city fast enough to save the campaign and carefully enough to save the prize, and the defender has built a battle where those two demands pull against each other in every street.

objectives.primary: Clear the industrial city and break the garrison, taking the manufacturing core mostly intact before the campaign's budget and timetable run out.
objectives.secondary: Take the works whole. Keep the foundries, tooling, and skilled workers functioning, not smashed to rubble in the clearing.
objectives.bonus: Split the garrison's local volunteers from the Republic-remnant core, turned, surrendered, or taken out, so the defense breaks faster and the city is governable after.

complications.name: The City Is the Trap
complications.text: The garrison fights to make the taking ruinous, not to win. Every strongpoint, every ambush, every fortified factory is placed to cost the assault the most and slow it the most, trading the city for the {EMPLOYER}'s wider campaign.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The defenders aim to maximize the assault's casualties and time rather than to hold ground for its own sake. The defense is graded on what it costs the attacker, and the garrison gives up positions only once they have taken their toll. A campaign-culmination clock advances with the assault's losses and elapsed time.

complications.name: The Prize Must Survive
complications.text: The industrial core is both the objective and the limit on how you can fight. Clear it with fire and you win the streets but throw away the foundries the campaign exists to take. The defenders fight from inside the works precisely because the {EMPLOYER} cannot burn them out.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Heavy-weapon and area fire in the industrial core damages the secondary objective and the world's value after the campaign. The defenders mass in the works to exploit the {EMPLOYER}'s reluctance to fire. Clearing it intact means close fighting, at a casualty and time cost the culmination clock counts.

complications.name: The Campaign Clock
complications.text: The reclamation runs on a Parliament budget and a watching province. Every week the second city holds burns money and credibility the campaign cannot spare, and the garrison is counting the weeks as a weapon.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A campaign-culmination clock runs against the assault, advanced by time and losses. If it runs out before the city falls, the wider campaign stalls, funding or political will fails, and the assault becomes untenable no matter the tactical position. Both speed and economy feed the clock, and the defender's whole plan is to run it out.

decisionPoints.name: How to Clear the City
decisionPoints.context: The works must be taken whole, the garrison broken, and the campaign clock beaten: three demands the defender has arranged to pull against each other in every street. The clearing method you choose now decides whether the {EMPLOYER} inherits a working city, a ruin, or a stalled campaign.

options.title: Clear It Block by Block
advantages: Clear the city carefully, strongpoint by strongpoint, with minimal heavy fire near the works: the surest way to take the industrial core intact
Keeps the assault's casualties down by refusing to rush prepared positions
A carefully cleared city is a held city, defensible behind the assault
disadvantages: Careful is slow, and the campaign clock is the defender's chosen weapon, so a city taken intact but late is a campaign stalled
Block-by-block clearing against a defense built to take its toll is a long grind that burns weeks
Every careful day is a day the {EMPLOYER}'s budget and credibility drain
options.consequence: You take the city the right way and race the clock the defender set. The works come through whole if the clock lasts, and the garrison's whole bet is that careful is slow and slow is fatal to the campaign.

costs.resource: the campaign-culmination clock, drawn down by the weeks careful clearing costs
costs.risk: the city falls intact but too late, the campaign runs out in the rubble, and a battlefield victory becomes a strategic defeat

options.title: Fast Combined-Arms Thrust
advantages: Drive a concentrated combined-arms thrust to the city's heart fast, splitting the defense and taking the key works before the garrison can make the whole city costly
Speed beats the campaign clock and denies the defender the long grind it wants
A fast cut to the industrial core may collapse the defense from the center out
disadvantages: A fast thrust through prepared urban ground runs the assault into the ambushes the defender built for exactly this
Speed in the works risks the heavy fire that wrecks the prize
A thrust that stalls in the center is an assault cut off in the heart of a fortress city
options.consequence: You trade caution for speed and bet a fast cut to the heart beats both the clock and the defense. The pace saves the campaign, if the thrust does not stall in the ambushes or wreck the works it races to take.

costs.resource: the works' intact value and the assault's cohesion, risked driving fast through prepared urban defenses
costs.risk: the thrust stalls in the ambush belt, or the heavy fighting in the works wrecks the prize, losing the city or the reason for it

options.title: Split the Volunteers First
advantages: The local volunteers stiffening the garrison are fighting for their city, not for the Republic remnant. Reach them, and the defense may crack from within before the assault has to grind through it
Splitting the volunteers from the core thins the defense and shortens the battle
A city whose own people stop fighting is taken faster and wholer, and is more governable after: the bonus objective made decisive
disadvantages: Reaching the volunteers mid-assault is slow and uncertain, and the Republic core may purge them or stiffen their resolve
The volunteers may want the city for themselves, not for the {EMPLOYER}, which could complicate the peace
Time spent on the approach is time the campaign clock keeps counting
options.consequence: You attack the defense's weak seam instead of its strength, betting the city's own people can be peeled off the remnant holding it. If the volunteers break for home, the battle shortens and the works survive. If they hold, the {EMPLOYER} has spent clock to learn the seam was welded shut.

costs.resource: the campaign clock and the assault's momentum, spent courting volunteers who may hold anyway
costs.risk: the volunteers stay with the core or take the city for themselves, and the approach has burned clock to change nothing

decisionPoints.name: The Foundry Strongpoint
decisionPoints.context: The garrison's strongest position is the central foundry complex, the heart of the works and the heart of the defense, dug in deep, and the one position whose fall breaks the city. Take it whole and you win the campaign's prize. Wreck it and you lose the campaign. Leave it and the campaign stalls.

options.title: Storm It Intact
advantages: Take the foundry by close assault, infantry and 'Mechs clearing it hall by hall, holding fire discipline to spare the furnaces and tooling
The foundry whole is the prize the whole campaign was for
Its fall breaks the city's defense at the center
disadvantages: A close assault on the strongest dug-in position in the city is the bloodiest fight of the battle
Fire discipline in a desperate close fight is hard to hold, and one heavy exchange turns the furnaces to slag
The garrison defends the foundry harder than anywhere else, because it knows the {EMPLOYER} will not burn it
options.consequence: You pay the battle's highest price to take the prize whole. The foundry falls intact and the city with it, or the close fight wrecks the furnaces the campaign crossed the stars for, and the bill is paid in the assault's best either way.

costs.resource: the assault's strength at its highest cost, spent storming the city's strongest position at close range
costs.risk: the close fight wrecks the foundry it was meant to take whole, and the assault wins a gutted prize at the battle's worst price

options.title: Cut It Off, Don't Storm It
advantages: Surround the foundry, clear the rest of the city around it, and starve or force its garrison out without storming the works directly
Spares the furnaces by refusing the close fight inside them
Lets the rest of the city fall while the strongpoint withers
disadvantages: Surrounding it is slow, and a besieged strongpoint at the city's heart costs clock the campaign does not have
A surrounded garrison fighting from the works can hold long past when the campaign needs the city
The defenders may wreck the foundry themselves rather than surrender it
options.consequence: You refuse the foundry's close fight and try to take it by patience instead of fire. The works survive your restraint, if the defenders' own patience and the campaign's clock do not outlast the siege inside the siege.

costs.resource: the campaign clock, spent slowly surrounding the central strongpoint while the rest of the city is cleared
costs.risk: the surrounded garrison holds past the campaign's deadline or wrecks the foundry itself, and patience loses the city or the prize

options.title: Force a Surrender
advantages: Offer the foundry's garrison terms, honorable surrender, the volunteers paroled home, the works spared, and break the strongpoint without storming it
A negotiated fall takes the foundry whole, fast, and with the workers intact
Splits the volunteers from the remnant at the decisive point and makes the city governable after
disadvantages: The Republic-remnant core may refuse terms and fight to the end anyway, spending the clock on talks that fail
Terms offered and then broken, by either side, poison the rest of the assault and the peace
A garrison that suspects a trick may wreck the foundry rather than trust the offer
options.consequence: You try to win the prize with words at the point where fire would ruin it. The foundry falls whole and the city with it if the terms hold, or the talks burn clock the campaign cannot spare and end with the close fight the offer was meant to avoid.

costs.resource: the campaign clock and the assault's credibility, staked on terms the remnant may refuse
costs.risk: the surrender offer fails or is read as a trick, the foundry is stormed or wrecked anyway, and the talks cost the time that made them worth trying

entries.event: Alarm: the assault crosses the start line into the city's outer industrial ring. The garrison's forward positions open up from prepared strongpoints and the block-by-block fight begins. The defenders give ground only for a price.
First major strongpoint contacted in a factory complex. The assault's choice, grind it down, bypass and surround it, or rush it, sets the pattern for the battle and the rate the campaign clock burns.
Anti-'Mech ambushes in the street canyons take their toll. The defender's design, cost and delay over ground, becomes plain. The works loom ahead, defenders dug into the very furnaces.
Local volunteer positions are spotted, separate from the Republic-remnant strongpoints. This is the seam in the defense, and the window to work it is visible.
The assault reaches the central foundry complex, the city's heart and the defense's strongest ground. The decision on how to take the prize can no longer wait.
Campaign-culmination assessment: the city taken or stalled, the works intact or wrecked, the budget and political will spent or holding. The second city decides the whole reclamation.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The deadline is the campaign, not any single clock. The hard limit is culmination: when the {EMPLOYER}'s budget, timetable, and political will run out, the reclamation stalls and the assault becomes untenable wherever it stands, and the garrison has won by making one city cost the whole war. But culmination is only half the deadline. A city taken late stalls the campaign, and a city taken in ruins throws away its prize. The assault must clear the second city fast enough to save the campaign and carefully enough to save the works, against a defender who built the battle so that one of those two failures is always the easier trap, and who is counting the {EMPLOYER}'s weeks as the real measure of the war.

opforSketch.composition: A reinforced {TARGET_FACTION} garrison battalion fighting an urban attrition defense: a BattleMech company (Regular, dug into factory strongpoints and street-canyon ambushes), an armor company in prepared and ambush positions plus combat engineers who have fortified the industrial sprawl (this is the combined-arms weight — ambush armor and engineer-built strongpoints throughout the works), and infantry — Republic-remnant regulars stiffened by local volunteers — throughout the built-up core. The defining asset is the fortified city, not the numbers. Behavioral breakpoint: the regulars fight to extract maximum cost and delay, ceding positions only when paid for; the local volunteers' commitment is the seam — they fight for their city and may break, surrender, or turn under pressure or terms.
opforSketch.behavior: The garrison fights an attrition-and-time war, not a battle for victory. It holds prepared strongpoints to bleed the assault, ambushes the street canyons, fortifies the works to exploit the {EMPLOYER}'s reluctance to destroy the prize, and trades the city for the {EMPLOYER}'s wider campaign — every week held is a week of the enemy's budget burned. Its aim is to make the second city cost the whole war. Its weaknesses are the volunteers who fight for the city rather than the remnant holding it, and the prize itself, which the garrison must defend without wrecking if it hopes for terms — the same constraint that binds the attacker binds the defender too.

forks.name: OPERATION WORKING CITY
forks.trigger: The second city cleared and the garrison broken with the works intact, inside the campaign's window.
forks.consequence: The manufacturing heart of {WORLD} is the {EMPLOYER}'s, the reclamation saved by the city that nearly broke it — and the unit holds the won city through its restless first months, the foundries restarting under {EMPLOYER} oversight, the surviving garrison and the volunteers a resistance waiting to see whether the new order is worth more than the old.

forks.name: OPERATION STALLED CAMPAIGN
forks.trigger: The campaign culminates before the city falls, or the works are wrecked in the taking.
forks.consequence: The garrison achieves exactly what it intended: a second city that cost the whole reclamation. The {EMPLOYER}'s campaign stalls in the rubble, Parliament's will fails, and the follow-on is a withdrawal off a half-taken world — the unit covering the retreat of a campaign the second city defeated.

forks.name: OPERATION HOLLOW WORKS
forks.trigger: The city is taken but the works are substantially damaged, or the volunteers turn the city against the occupier after the fall.
forks.consequence: The {EMPLOYER} holds a second city whose foundries are wreckage and whose people fight on in the streets — a prize taken and ruined, a campaign won on the map and bleeding on the ground. The unit must hold and rebuild a gutted city while the volunteers who fought for it once fight the occupier now.

storyElementSeed: In a factory hall cleared an hour ago, an {EMPLOYER} trooper finds the foundry's shift roster still chalked on a board by the door — names, machines, the next shift's start time, written before the war reached the works. Below it, in a different hand, someone has added the date the fighting started and nothing after. He looks at the cold furnaces the assault was ordered not to break, and at the names, and does not wipe the board.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Take the second city whole and break its garrison before the campaign runs out of road. The works are the reason Parliament voted this war, and a foundry in ruins is a vote the provincialists will quote for a decade. Clear it fast enough to save the campaign and clean enough to save the prize, or we will have spent the whole reclamation on one city's rubble.

resourceGates.lackingText: You have no munitions depot to keep a high-tempo thrust supplied. A fast drive through the city outruns its own ammunition resupply. Either add the cost of open-market stock bought before the assault, or accept that the thrust slows to the rate the magazines allow at exactly the wrong moment.

You have no secure facility to hold and process a surrendered garrison. Accepting terms leaves hundreds of prisoners and paroled volunteers with nowhere to put them under guard. Accept a drain on the assault's strength to manage them in the middle of an unfinished battle.
